title: Zusammenfassung EDPB Guidelines on Anonymisation
abstract: Die Präsentation fasst die EDPB Guidelines 02/2026 on Anonymisation (Version 1, 7. Juli 2026, öffentliche Konsultation) aus der Perspektive von Forschungsdatenzentren zusammen und bewertet sie kritisch. Zentral ist das Konzept der relativen Anonymität. Die Frage, ob Daten anonym sind, muss demzufolge je Entität und Kontext geprüft werden. title: Windowed Hankel KEM: implementation, challenge instances and evidence for Windowed Hankel LWE
abstract: Reference and constant-time native implementations of Windowed Hankel KEM, challenge instances of the Windowed Hankel LWE problem, and the scripts and recorded outputs behind every figure of the accompanying paper, Windowed Hankel LWE: A Structured-LWE Problem for Cryptanalysis, with a Compact KEM. Windowed Hankel LWE is a structured variant of LWE whose public matrix is a Hankel matrix generated by one long pseudorandom sequence. Its hardness is an assumption: the known Middle-Product LWE reductions do not apply. The paper offers it as a problem for cryptanalysis; the KEM is research code and not for production use.

title: Türkçe ABSA’da Büyük Dil Modeli Tabanlı Otomatik Etiketleme: Başarılar ve Zorluklar
abstract: Bu araştırma, Türkçe restoran yorumlarında Hedefe Yönelik Duygu Analizi kapsamında, GPT-4o tabanlı otomatik etiketlemenin manuel etiketlemeye (SemEval) kıyasla etkinliğini incelemektedir. Araştırmada hedef terim çıkarımı (ATE), kategori ve duygu sınıflandırma alt görevleri; SVM, BiLSTM, MLP ve BERTurk modelleri kullanılarak SemEval, GPT-4o ve Birleştirilmiş veri düzenlerinde değerlendirilmiştir. Deneysel karşılaştırma, otomatik etiketlerin tek başına ve manuel veri ile birlikte kullanıldığında farklı görevlerde nasıl bir performans profili oluşturduğunu ortaya koymayı hedeflemektedir. Bulgulara göre, ATE görevinde SemEval üzerinde SVM yüksek geri çağırım ile öne çıkmıştır (Recall=0,8463; F1=0,7265). Duygu sınıflandırmasında en yüksek başarıya Birleştirilmiş düzende BERTurk ile ulaşılmıştır (F1=0,8336; doğruluk=0,9255); bu sonuç, daha geniş ve çeşitli veride bağlamsal temsillerin avantajını desteklemektedir. Kategori sınıflandırmasında ise en iyi sonuçlar Birleştirilmiş düzende SVM (F1=0,5183) ve BERTurk (F1=0,5108) tarafından üretilmiş; sınıf sayısının yüksek ve sınırların bulanık olduğu bu görevde performansın daha sınırlı kaldığı görülmüştür. Genel olarak sonuçlar, otomatik etiketlemenin özellikle duygu gibi daha net sınıf sınırlarına sahip görevlerde rekabetçi bir veri kaynağı sunduğunu; kategori gibi daha zor görevlerde ise etiket tutarlılığı, sınıf dengesizliği ve görev-model uyumunun belirleyici olduğunu göstermektedir. Bu çalışma, farklı model ailelerini birlikte karşılaştırarak otomatik etiketli verinin hangi koşullarda daha güvenilir biçimde kullanılabileceğine ilişkin pratik bir değerlendirme çerçevesi sunmaktadır.

title: Orchestration Frameworks for Agentic AI
abstract: This chapter focuses on orchestration frameworks for coordinating sophisticated agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems within single connected and autonomous vehicle (CAV) systems, covering graph-based orchestration (LangGraph) and dialogue-based orchestration (AutoGen). The chapter examines theoretical foundations, practical implementations, and comparative analysis of these orchestration paradigms. LangGraph provides deterministic, verifiable workflows suitable for safety-critical applications, while AutoGen offers flexibility and adaptability for complex, dynamic scenarios. The chapter covers workflow design, state management, error handling, and integration patterns. It provides comprehensive comparison and selection guidance for choosing appropriate frameworks for specific CAV applications, emphasizing how orchestration mechanisms enable the practical implementation and deployment of agentic AI capabilities.

title: Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models
abstract: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.

title: LunaTP: Enabling Efficient and Scalable Tensor Product for Equivariant MLIPs
abstract: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise atomistic simulations with accuracy approaching that of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the high computational cost of their core Clebsch--Gordan tensor product (CGTP) convolutions severely limits model scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we rethink the parallel execution of CGTP convolutions and introduce LunaTP. Built on node-centric execution, LunaTP exploits path-group parallelism and multi-level reuse to accelerate CGTP convolutions and higher-order derivative computation while preserving the underlying mathematical formulation. On an NVIDIA H100 GPU, LunaTP achieves kernel speedups of up to 250.0$\times$ over e3nn and 17.1$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. It also delivers end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7$\times$ over e3nn and 3.11$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. Finally, LunaTP demonstrates scalability and robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, delivering substantial acceleration for training and atomistic simulation with high-accuracy equivariant MLIPs.

title: Certifying Almost-Sure Reachability in Unknown MDPs
abstract: {\em Specification-Guided Reinforcement Learning (RL)} has largely concerned itself with \emph{learning} an optimal policy against a formal specification in an unknown {\em Markov Decision Process (MDP)}. We take up the dual question. Given a policy already in hand, can one \emph{verify} that it is correct against a formal specification in an unknown MDP, using sampling access alone? Such a question arises naturally in safety-critical systems. We investigate it for the {\em almost-sure reachability property}, whose correctness is witnessed by a {\em ranking supermartingale (RSM)} certificate. Our first finding is negative. In the absence of any further information about the MDP, one can neither learn such a certificate nor verify a candidate one with probabilistic guarantees. On the positive side, we show that, under a mild restriction, a known lower bound $p_{\min}$ on nonzero transition probabilities, a correct certificate \emph{can} be learned with PAC-style guarantees. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of learning and verifying certificates for almost-sure reachability in unknown MDPs from sampling access alone. Finally, our experiments show that the $p_{\min}$-based sufficient condition, while sound, is conservative: the learned certificate often remains valid on the true MDP even when the condition fails.

title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.

title: Neural Dimensional Analysis: Foundations of Dimensionless and Scale-Consistent Computation
abstract: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.

Jadvalli ma'lumotlar tarkibida uchraydigan bo'sh qiymatlar, noto'g'ri kiritilgan hamda predmet sohasi uchun mantiqan yaroqsiz bo'lgan anomal qiymatlar klassifikatsiya modellarining samaradorligiga salbiy ta'sir ko'rsatishi mumkin. Mazkur muammoni bartaraf etish maqsadida belgining turi, ruxsat etilgan qiymatlar sohasi va obyektning sinf tegini hisobga oluvchi algoritmik yondashuv taklif etilgan. Algoritmda sonli va tartibli belgilar uchun mediana, nominal va binar belgilar uchun esa moda qiymatidan foydalaniladi. Bunda statistik qiymatlar butun dataset asosida emas, faqat o'qitish to'plamidagi to'g'ri qiymatlar asosida shakllantiriladi. Bu esa test ma'lumotlarining o'qitish jarayoniga bilvosita ta'sir ko'rsatishi, ya'ni ma'lumotlarning sizib chiqishi xavfini kamaytiradi.

title: Bee Swarm: CV>0 Autonomous Evolution Protocol - Implementation (verify-2-8-v1.0.0: language emergence, section 3.8)
abstract: PHP implementation of the CV>0 Autonomous Evolution Protocol. This release formalizes protocol section 3.8 (language emergence) as a one-command measurement: the compressor distills isomorphic laws from two synthetic domains into one self-named grammar atom, and that atom solves a third domain that raw search cannot solve at matched depth and beam (R1b); a random atom does not solve it (R1c, specificity); compilation is not worse than the coalition on held-out slices. Bounded claim: the acquired operator enabled a solution under the given search constraints. Equal compute cost is NOT claimed (with-atom 6.1 s vs raw-matched 2.1 s; atom-birth 0.001 s). Universal superiority is NOT claimed. CV 9.99 in report rows with found=false is the NOT_FOUND sentinel. Synthetic fixture; not independently replicated (independent re-implementation invited, see repository issues). Reproduce: composer install; php scripts/verify_2_8.php. Committed report and evidence: Benchmarks/verify_2_8/. Suite: 1226 tests two-pass green. Protocol: DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23287007 (v2.1). Erratum 1 (2026-10-13): documentation-only correction: test count in the release notes corrected (1224 to 1226, two-pass rc6), evidence.json suite/RAM notes synced to the final gate (peak memory was recorded), release-candidate wording removed. Frozen results, report.json, and the v1.0.0 MANIFEST hashes are unchanged; see ERRATUM_1.md.

title: Confidence-Aware Explainable AI for Reliable Large Language Model Decision Support
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in decision-support systems because of their ability to interpret complex queries, synthesize information, and generate contextually relevant responses. However, their use in reliability sensitive settings remains challenging because LLMs can produce incorrect or unsupported outputs while expressing a high degree of linguistic confidence. This paper presents a confidence aware explainable AI framework for improving the reliability of LLM-based decision support. The proposed approach combines model confidence, semantic consistency across multiple stochastic generations, and explanation support to construct a composite reliability score. A selective decision module then uses this score to determine whether a generated response should be accepted, flagged for review, or withheld through abstention. The framework is evaluated across factual, commonsense, and multi-step reasoning tasks using multiple open-weight LLMs. Performance is assessed in terms of answer accuracy, expected calibration error, failure-detection AUROC, selective accuracy, and response coverage. The evaluation investigates whether combining complementary reliability signals provides a more informative assessment of response correctness than self-reported confidence, model confidence, or semantic consistency alone. The proposed framework provides a practical reliability layer for LLM-based decision-support systems by jointly communicating confidence, explanation support, and an actionable response decision, thereby helping distinguish sufficiently reliable outputs from those requiring further verification or abstention.

title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
abstract: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).

title: WAVE-0: Bridging VLA Policies and WAMs with Lightweight Latent Future Prediction
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. We introduce WAVE-0 (World-model-Augmented VLA Execution), a framework that bridges VLAs and WAMs through a lightweight latent world model. By connecting the semantic understanding of pretrained VLAs with explicit future prediction, WAVE-0 allows anticipated action consequences to directly guide action generation. Built on a pretrained VLA, its 257M world model translates VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition the action expert, unifying latent planning, future prediction, and action generation. The world model is trained directly on ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, requiring neither pixel reconstruction nor large-scale video pretraining. WAVE-0 achieves success rates of 91.47% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.7% on LIBERO, along with 88.0%, 61.4%, and 75.0% on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and LIBERO-Para, respectively. On real-world tasks, it improves the success rate of π_{0.5} from 38.3% to 73.3%. These results demonstrate strong manipulation performance and generalization across diverse distribution shifts.

title: Beyond RMSE and Granger Gain: Multi-Horizon Forecast-Error Entropy for Nonlinear Predictive Coupling
abstract: We investigate whether the past of an auxiliary time series provides predictive information about a target beyond that contained in the target's own history. We compare matched out-of-sample target-only and target-plus-source forecasts and introduce the forecast-error distribution entropy (FEDE) predictive-causality framework, where predictive causality is understood in the Granger sense: auxiliary history is informative when it improves prediction beyond the target's own past. FEDE quantifies how the full signed forecast-error distribution changes across prediction horizons. Controlled nonlinear benchmarks hide source-target dependence behind nonlinear transformations not supplied to the predictors. LightGBM recovers these hidden channels, whereas Ridge does not. Across four equal-power nonlinearities and four noise levels, the mean response-sensitivity statistic for FEDE remains 29.00, 27.47, 23.22, and 28.67, compared with 14.09, 10.68, 12.67, and 12.71 for mean log-RMSE gain. Directional and source controls separate the true source-to-target channel from the reverse direction and from independent periodic, quasiperiodic, chaotic, and autoregressive auxiliaries. Chronological Granger-style comparisons show strong model-form dependence: a degree-2 polynomial model is exceptionally sensitive to the matched quadratic channel but becomes weak or oppositely aligned for other nonlinearities, while basic convergent cross mapping is weak or directionally inconsistent in this stochastic, partly non-invertible setting. FEDE remains positively aligned across all 108 tested combinations of window length, history length, and maximum forecast horizon. Together, these results establish FEDE as a sensitive and robust horizon-resolved tool that extracts predictive information beyond conventional error-magnitude measures when the nonlinear interaction form is unknown. Code available in Zenodo.

title: The Image Still Has a Say: Final-Answer Repair for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
abstract: Although chain-of-thought prompting has improved multimodal reasoning, it is still difficult to produce correct final answers, as the reasoning can drift away from the image. Besides, the trace is already fixed when the answer is generated, leaving no room for self-correction. Considering the image is still available at the final-answer step, we think it is reasonable to fix the answer there without rewriting the reasoning. As such, the problem becomes to correct the final answer using the image under fixed reasoning. Unlike methods that improve trace generation through training, resampling, or decoding-time grounding, we repair the final-answer readout while keeping the reasoning trace fixed. The motivation is based on our finding that a wrong option can become prematurely committed in the reasoning while the correct option still has stronger image support in middle-to-deep layers. Thus, we propose Text-to-Visual Evidence Reallocation (TVER), a training-free method for final-answer repair. Specifically, TVER selects answer-related text and question-matched image patches, and moves bounded attention from text to patches. Furthermore, the patches are chosen in a middle-to-deep layer window based on question relevance. Our method improves answers across benchmarks and backbones, with gains in both multiple-choice and open-answer evaluations.

title: PACT: A Pragmatic Prompting Framework for Expressive and Voice-Preserving Speech-to-Speech Translation
abstract: Speech-to-speech translation should preserve not only what is said, but also who says it and how it is said. Existing end-to-end S2ST, speech MLLM, and cascade systems can preserve content or timbre, but often struggle to realize emotion, tone, rhythm, pauses, and pragmatic attitude in the target language. We propose PACT, a target-space pragmatic prompting framework for expressive and voice-preserving S2ST. PACT extracts source pragmatic cues, projects them into the target-language expression space, calibrates the projected representation to a realizable target subspace, and converts it into continuous prompts for a frozen speech generator. On bidirectional Spanish-English TOPI evaluation, PACT achieves the best overall performance among evaluated systems across content fidelity, voice preservation, and expression preservation metrics.

title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. SQUELCH adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, SQUELCH improves over LoRA by 2.2--3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8--1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.

title: Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine
abstract: The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Each thinking step is an attracting but strongly non-normal map exhibiting balanced amplification (Murphy and Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initialization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach's theorem, the neural state has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve's motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R^2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.

title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
abstract: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.

title: Application of a convolutional neural network for automatic cytological diagnosis of 7 common canine tumors on whole slide images: a proof-of-concept
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence may help improve speed and consistency of diagnostic veterinary cytology, but validated tools remain limited. Objectives To develop and evaluate a convolutional neural network (CNN) for automatic classification of 7 common canine tumors on cytology whole-slide images (WSIs). Methods Ninety-one May–Grünwald Giemsa–stained canine cytology cases were selected, representing carcinoma, histiocytoma, lymphoma, mast cell tumor, melanoma, plasma cell tumor, and soft tissue sarcoma, together with a background class. Slides were tiled into 22,577 image patches (512 × 512 pixels) and manually labeled and split using a case-wise 3-fold design to avoid data leakage. An ImageNet-pretrained Inception-v3 CNN was fine-tuned for 8-class classification. Performance was assessed at tile level, Grad-CAM was used for qualitative interpretability analysis, and majority-vote prediction was further evaluated at ROI level using attention-guided inference and at WSI level using attention-free whole-slide inference. Results Mean test accuracy at tile level was 86.3%, with mean macro balanced accuracy of 92.0% and mean macro F1-score of 85.6%. Grad-CAM showed attention focused predominantly on cytologically relevant cellular regions. At ROI level, attention-guided inference achieved 100% Top1 accuracy (28/28 cases). At WSI level, attention-free whole-slide inference achieved 92.9% Top1 accuracy (26/28 cases), and the correct diagnosis was included within the top 3 predictions in all cases. Conclusion Inception-v3 achieved high diagnostic performance on canine cytology WSIs. The results support the feasibility of both AI-assisted ROI-based decision support and fully automated whole-slide inference in veterinary cytology. These findings are proof-of-concept evidence from a curated, single-institution cohort of typical, well-differentiated cases and require validation on diagnostically challenging and external cases before clinical use.

title: Shortest Constructions Predict Evolutionary Searchability Across Universal Binary Operators
abstract: Single universal operators such as EML generate every elementary function from one binary operation. We show that evolutionary search assembles trees of about the same size, roughly 12–13 nodes at our reference budget, whichever operator is used. So what makes an operator easy or hard to search isn't what it computes, but which functions it makes short. We prove the shortest constructions of common functions for seven operators, and show that one size curve predicts how often search finds any function under any operator. One operator (EDL) is a measurable exception. The practical message: choose the operator whose shortest constructions cover your functions, because universality alone says nothing about searchability.

title: A collaborative multi-agent architecture with physics-consistency validation for robust microseismic signal classification
abstract: Reliable classification of microseismic (MS) records is essential for geohazard early warning in deep underground construction. Corrupted or missing local observations can distort shared multi-sensor representations, and waveform similarity alone is often insufficient to separate engineering disturbances from MS events. This study proposes Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (PI-MARL), a sensor-bound framework for classifying MS events, blasting signals, and interference signals. Each sensor channel is processed by an independent agent comprising a lightweight multi-scale 1D-CNN and a dueling deep Q-network. Agents exchange latent representations through hierarchical spatio-temporal attention organized by front and back sensor groups. A separate physics-consistency module validates preliminary MS proposals using inter-group arrival-time and characteristic-band spectral conditions when both groups yield valid observations; in single-group operation, only the spectral condition is applied. Inter-group energy distribution serves solely as supplementary propagation evidence and does not by itself determine acceptance. Training combines the task reward with a fixed penalty for physics-violating proposals and attention-weighted credit assignment. Over ten runs on a held-out test subset from an active deep-tunnel project, PI-MARL attained a mean (± standard deviation) macro F1-score of 97.48 ± 0.29%, macro recall of 97.23 ± 0.38%, and false alarm rate (FAR) of 0.81 ± 0.28%. FAR increased to 10.0% in the lowest evaluated signal-to-noise ratio interval, [10, 15) dB. With four of the eight sensors unavailable, FAR was approximately 2.5% when failures were randomly distributed and both groups retained valid observations, and 6.8% under complete front-group failure, where the framework ran in single-group mode. Relative to the evaluated baselines, degradation was more gradual as noise and sensor loss increased, indicating that the coordinated architecture remains effective under the engineering conditions examined here.

title: FireGraphNet: Sub-daily wildfire spread prediction with directed graph neural networks
abstract: Wildfire decisions are made in hours, yet most learned spread models predict daily on targets including burned area. We propose FireGraphNet which formulates 12-hour growth as node classification on directed H3 graphs, with candidates ahead of the front and wind alignment, terrain, fuel continuity and barriers on edges. On satellite perimeters it achieves average precision 1.7-1.9x the strongest distance baseline on test California fires and 1.62x out of state. We show this skill comes from message passing rather than cell features or the aggregator, is highest on young fires in state, is carried deep along the wind by its edges, and is hidden by pooling. A convolutional network matches this ranking once trained on new growth, at worse calibration, so candidate construction, target definition, and aggregation shape conclusions about model skill. Editing fuel and barrier attributes reduces predicted spread more under guided than random placement, extending FireGraphNet to operational intervention analysis.

title: Recasting DiT for Extreme Image Compression with Hierarchical Visual Priors
abstract: Pretrained diffusion models provide powerful generative priors for extreme image compression, but their stochastic, iterative generation processes are not designed to decode compressed representations directly. We present PrismCodec, which recasts a pretrained Diffusion Transformer (DiT) as a bitstream-grounded one-step generative decoder. PrismCodec uses the decoded representation in two complementary roles: a projected codec state defines the starting state for generation, while hierarchical visual priors derived from the same decoded latent provide semantic and structural guidance. To bridge the gap between stochastic, iterative generation and deterministic one-step decoding, we develop a progressive adaptation strategy. We first learn codec-conditioned transport from a noisy neighborhood centered on the codec state, distill it into a one-step mapping, and finally anneal the source perturbation to zero during end-to-end optimization. The resulting decoder reconstructs deterministically from the received representation without additional conditioning bits. Across Kodak, CLIC, and DIV2K, PrismCodec consistently improves rate-perception performance over prior generative codecs, achieving BD-rate reductions of 70-75% in LPIPS and 75-81% in DISTS over StableCodec. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Adaptive Variance-Reduced Stochastic Sequential (Quadratic Constrained) Quadratic Programming
abstract: In this paper, we propose an adaptive variance-reduced stochastic sequential (quadratic constrained) quadratic programming (AVR-SS(QC)QP) method for nonlinear constrained optimization. The framework integrates SPIDER-based variance reduction, stochastic quasi-Newton curvature information, merit-function globalization, and adaptive switching between stochastic SQP and SQCQP models. The switching mechanism is governed by a relative constraint model curvature indicator that measures the second-order constraint information neglected by the linearized SQP model. A smoothed hysteresis rule ac?tivates the SQCQP model only when the relative constraint curvature is significant. An exact L1 merit function with Armijo backtracking globalizes the resulting directions, while a coupled stochastic Lyapunov analysis controls the interaction between gradient-estimation error and optimization progress. Under standard smoothness, sampling, regularity, and second-order conditions, we establish almost-sure consistency of the variance-reduced gradient estimator and global convergence of the KKT residual. We further show that, near regular KKT points, the curvature indicator vanishes and the method eventually selects the computationally cheaper SQP model. Numerical experiments on a sparse principal component analysis problem illustrate the practical be?havior of the proposed framework.

title: SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction
abstract: Multimodal medical data captures complementary aspects of disease. It provides a comprehensive basis for diagnosis and the identification of biological associations linked to progression or treatment response. Established contrastive learning approaches exploit shared information across modalities, but fall short in exploiting complementary, modality-specific signals relevant for a task. Here, we propose a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE) framework that separates task-relevant unimodal and multimodal information from instance-specific variation task-irrelevant, allowing complementary signals across modalities to be leveraged for prediction. The method yields benefits even if modalities are missing at test time. We evaluate the method on a treatment response prediction task using medical imaging and RNA data. Empirical comparison with alignment-based and multimodal VAE state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates improved multimodal prediction performance, and consistent benefits for prediction from a single modality after multimodal training. The full code can be found here: https://github.com/cirmuw/SYNPRED.

title: MicroCLIP: Connecting Text and Microscopy Images via Contrastive Language--Image Pretraining
abstract: Understanding fluorescence microscopy images is fundamental to automating biological research. However, existing methods typically learn predefined concepts from closed-set data, limiting transfer across tasks and biological contexts. In this work, we introduce MicroCLIP, a vision-language model that learns generalizable cellular and subcellular representations from natural language supervision for open-set image classification and retrieval. To pretrain MicroCLIP, we construct MicroPool-2M, a dataset of approximately 2.5 million fluorescence microscopy image-text pairs spanning diverse cellular structures, cell lines, and imaging conditions. Aligning microscopy images with biological concepts in natural language is challenging because most images lack descriptive captions and biological knowledge annotations. We therefore progressively establish image-text associations at three levels to provide MicroCLIP with richer semantic supervision: (1) category-level alignment links images to standardized labels defined by subcellular structure-cell-line combinations; (2) knowledge-level alignment incorporates biological priors derived from these labels to capture relationships across species and cell types; and (3) detail-level alignment uses a multimodal large language model to recaption and verify image-text pairs at scale, emphasizing fine-grained visual characteristics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MicroCLIP achieves leading performance in zero-shot classification and text-image retrieval on microscopy images. It retrieves images with specific cellular characteristics from thousands of candidates and generalizes to unseen biological concepts without additional supervision. These results highlight MicroCLIP's potential as a foundation model for fluorescence microscopy.

title: ScenePercept: Scenario-Conditioned Perceptual Assessment of Real-World User-Generated Content Images
abstract: The rapid development of mobile imaging and social platforms has led to explosive growth in user-generated content images, making their systematic and comprehensive perceptual assessment increasingly important. Existing image perception benchmarks are typically task-oriented, curating specific scenarios for quality or aesthetic assessment and applying a uniform perceptual criterion across diverse scenarios. This limits their ability to capture the scene diversity and perceptual complexity of real-world UGC images. To address these limitations, we introduce ScenePercept-Bench, a benchmark designed to reflect the distribution of real-world UGC images, comprising 23,100 images across 21 categories and 105 fine-grained scenes. To account for the influence of scene context on human perception, we design a hierarchical, scene-aware annotation protocol, covering visual quality, aesthetic perception, and scene semantics, with 15 attributes in total. Each image is annotated with an overall score, 15 attribute-level scores, and structured explanatory reasoning. Building on this benchmark, we further introduce Scenario-Conditioned Perceptual Alignment, a training framework that tackles the heterogeneity of perceptual criteria across scenarios. SCPA jointly optimizes absolute score prediction, preference ranking, and cross-scenario calibration, preserving the model general perceptual assessment ability while encouraging it to explore and adapt perceptual criteria across different scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SCPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in UGC image perception and generalizes effectively to established IQA and IAA benchmarks.

title: When Does Opponent Modeling Pay Off? Spatial Inference Stabilises Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning agents in partially observable competitive games must act on beliefs about an unseen opponent's intent. We study a spatial opponent model: a transformer trained with hindsight-relabelled opponent goals that outputs a subgoal heatmap from the opponent's observed trajectory, fused early into a dueling double DQN. In symmetric constant-sum foraging games with partial observability, the module stabilises training. Plain TD(0) DQN suffers degenerate seeds in three of four one-step configurations, whereas the opponent-model agent never collapses and, wherever training succeeds, recovers the majority of the symmetric game value. Transfers zero-shot to a foraging opponent unseen by the learner, with a positive goal advantage over the baseline, and loses this edge exactly where an information argument predicts: against a full-information tracking adversary whose intent is the learner itself, and on resource-dense maps where both agents saturate. A blindfold ablation, zeroing the heatmap at deployment, decomposes the advantage into two mechanisms: training-time stabilisation, which dominates where the credit assignment is hard and survives blinding on the dense map, and deployment-time inference, whose reliance shrinks as fog thins on the sparse map. We conclude that opponent-goal inference is a stability-and-transfer mechanism whose value is governed by measurable boundary conditions: visibility (fog thickness), opponent intent, and resource density.

evidence.title: When Does Opponent Modeling Pay Off? Spatial Inference Stabilises Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
evidence.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning agents in partially observable competitive games must act on beliefs about an unseen opponent's intent. We study a spatial opponent model: a transformer trained with hindsight-relabelled opponent goals that outputs a subgoal heatmap from the opponent's observed trajectory, fused early into a dueling double DQN. In symmetric constant-sum foraging games with partial observability, the module stabilises training. Plain TD(0) DQN suffers degenerate seeds in three of four one-step configurations, whereas the opponent-model agent never collapses and, wherever training succeeds, recovers the majority of the symmetric game value. Transfers zero-shot to a foraging opponent unseen by the learner, with a positive goal advantage over the baseline, and loses this edge exactly where an information argument predicts: against a full-information tracking adversary whose intent is the learner itself, and on resource-dense maps where both agents saturate. A blindfold ablation, zeroing the heatmap at deployment, decomposes the advantage into two mechanisms: training-time stabilisation, which dominates where the credit assignment is hard and survives blinding on the dense map, and deployment-time inference, whose reliance shrinks as fog thins on the sparse map. We conclude that opponent-goal inference is a stability-and-transfer mechanism whose value is governed by measurable boundary conditions: visibility (fog thickness), opponent intent, and resource density.

title: How Inner Optimizers Shape Replica Scaling
abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) across geographically distributed and poorly interconnected compute pools or data centers has become a topic of significant interest. This has led to increased study of local optimization methods such as DiLoco for LLMs, especially those that use local (or inner) adaptive or preconditioned optimizers, which are critical for high-performance LLM training. However, a central challenge remains: it is well known that increasing the number of model replicas (replica scaling) while fixing the total training budget leads to monotonically decreasing performance. Existing work has empirically demonstrated that the choice of inner optimizer (Muon v.s. AdamW) can significantly improve this trend, but offers only limited explanation of the performance difference. In this work, we consider a range of inner-optimizers and identify two important factors that impact replica scaling: (1) the covariance structure of the pseudo-gradients and (2) the impact of batch size on the pseudogradient's noise scale. Based on these insights, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that whitening-based pre-conditioning is a powerful inner-optimizer desideratum. Our empirical evaluation extends the results to reveal that whitening-based inner-optimizers achieve strong replica scaling (for 8-96 replicas), with performance relative to DP improving as parameters and data are scaled.

title: Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text
abstract: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.

title: Enriching the EuSO ontology through GenAI-based terminological selection and conceptualisation
abstract: Abstract In academic and institutional contexts, the management and structuring of specialised knowledge are essential to support effective communication and internationalisation. Traditionally, ontology development and ontology-driven terminology work have relied on expert-based manual processes and corpus analysis techniques. However, recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) have opened new possibilities for supporting knowledge representation tasks. In this context, this study explores the use of a customised GenAI-based chatbot for assisting ontology development in the domain of European higher education. Specifically, The Ontology Assistant, built on ChatGPT-5.2 and enriched with a domain-specific corpus, was designed to support the identification and structuring of ontological categories within the EuroScholar Ontology (EuSO). The model’s performance was evaluated through six experimental runs using a gold standard derived from a selected ontological category. Precision, recall, and F1-measure were used to assess category retrieval. The results show consistent behaviour across runs, characterised by high recall and low precision, reflecting the exploratory capacity of the chatbot to identify candidate ontological categories. These findings suggest that GenAI chatbots can function as useful support tools within ontology development workflows, provided that expert intervention is applied to verify and maintain alignment with the EuSO.

title: Who Does the Model Miss? Auditing Territorial and Ethnic Equity in Hospital-Mortality Prediction with One Million Ecuadorian Discharge Records
abstract: Machine-learning risk scores are entering health decision-making, but a model that is accurate on average can still fail systematically for specific populations. We study in-hospital mortality prediction on the complete 2024 Ecuadorian hospital-discharge registry (1,132,667 records, 17,724 deaths, 1.56% prevalence), openly published by the national statistics institute. Because the registry codes the ICD-10 cause as the definitive discharge diagnosis, we exclude it from the deployable model and report a strictly admission-time specification. Every discharge receives an out-of-fold prediction, so the audit rests on hundreds of events per subgroup rather than tens. Class-weighted gradient boosting proves severely miscalibrated (expected calibration error 0.275, calibration intercept $$-4.02$$ ); isotonic recalibration fixes this (ECE 0.0001) and lets us select an operating point from a declared review budget instead of an arbitrary 0.5 cut. The calibrated model reaches ROC-AUC 0.854 and PR-AUC 0.100, about six times the prevalence floor. Our contribution is the equity audit with uncertainty. Detection differs by 9.7 points between mestizo and Indigenous patients (95% CI 5.3–13.9, $$p<0.001$$ ) and by 8.0 points by insurance status, whereas the urban–rural gap is not significant (0.7 points, CI $$-1.4$$ –2.7). Across provinces of residence, recall ranges from 0.09 to 0.60. Gaps concentrate intersectionally—Indigenous rural patients are the least well detected group—and persist when ethnicity and province are removed from the features, so they are not an artefact of encoding protected attributes. Group-specific thresholds, selected on held-out data, cut the ethnic gap to 1.6 points at a quantified cost in review workload. We release all code and use only public data, and argue that subgroup and territorial equity auditing, reported with confidence intervals, must be a first-class result in health AI built on open national data.

title: The noise cost of reservoir locality in broadband quantum amplifier chains
abstract: Directional quantum amplifiers enable weak-signal readout while protecting the source, but reservoir noise limits sensitivity. Finite-band suppression must reconcile frequency-dependent responses with fixed local couplings and finite rates. We construct adjacent-site loss channels attaining the known single-frequency minimum under local compatibility conditions, as an uncapped benchmark. For specified uniform and dimerized chains, we compare fixed reservoirs at matched drift, ports, high-gain band and complete gain/loss rate caps. At the representative cap $R=8$ and halfwidth $Ω=0.05$, nearest-neighbor arithmetic band average noise exceeds the unrestricted optimum by more than $1.01265$ quanta in the uniform chain for every finite $N\ge64$. Boundary-response bounds give necessary rates and targets requiring range two. At $N=64$, finite-auxiliary calculations retain a noise advantage under matched total coupling budgets; response bounds quantify noise-resolution tolerances. These theoretical results guide reservoir design and noise calibration for a proposed cryogenic microwave array with a $100$ kHz design band.

title: ReDiS: Reasoning-Diagnosis Self-Evolution for Multimodal Reasoning in Remote Sensing
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for remote sensing understanding, yet reliable reasoning remains challenging when tasks require fine-grained visual grounding and multi-step inference. Existing approaches typically rely on either costly pre-constructed reasoning trajectories or self-generated signals such as response consistency, which can reinforce shared errors and provide unreliable supervision. We introduce \textbf{Reasoning--Diagnosis Self-Evolution (ReDiS)}, a framework that separates reasoning exploration from candidate evaluation while allowing the two processes to evolve jointly. ReDiS instantiates two role-specific experts from a shared multimodal backbone: a \textbf{Reasoner} that explores diverse visual evidence--answer candidates and a \textbf{Diagnoser} that jointly evaluates the complete candidate set and provides credibility-aware feedback. As the Reasoner evolves, it exposes new candidate distributions and failure modes; the Diagnoser adapts to these changes and, in turn, reshapes the learning signal for subsequent exploration. To handle groups in which all sampled answers are incorrect and group-relative advantages vanish, we further introduce \textbf{Failure-Triggered Recovery (FTR)}, which provides minimal outcome-level correction without prescribing intermediate reasoning trajectories. Experiments on LHRS-Bench, MME-RS, and CHOICE show consistent improvements over Qwen3.5 backbones at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B scales. ReDiS improves category-averaged accuracy by 6.47 percentage points at 0.8B, while ReDiS-4B achieves the highest average performance among the compared remote sensing MLLMs.

title: A CaLLM Judge is a Better Judge: Mitigating Bias in LLM-as-a-judge
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to predict which of two candidate answers a human evaluator would prefer, providing a scalable alternative when human evaluation is too costly. Unfortunately, LLM judgments can exhibit systematic biases. Prior work has documented position, verbosity or model family of the candidate answers influencing the judge decision rather than their quality, while additional biases may remain undocumented. $\textit{Multicalibration}$ provides a natural framework to address this problem: each bias corresponds to miscalibration on an identifiable group, $\textit{e.g.}$, family bias manifests as overconfidence in answers generated by models belonging to the same family of the judge. The challenge is to fix miscalibration simultaneously across many, potentially unknown groups. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{CaLLM}$, a post hoc framework that multicalibrates an LLM judge, thereby bounding all such biases simultaneously. We prove that $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ bounds the bias of every group whose error structure is captured by an available representation, and that augmenting it with explicit bias groups further reduces the residual bias. We then derive theoretical conditions under which $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ improves the judge's accuracy, rather than trading it for calibration. Finally, we evaluate $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ across pairwise preference benchmarks, showing that it reduces the multicalibration error on both specified and unspecified bias groups, while improving predictive performance of the judge.

title: TStruct: Learning Shared Temporal Structures for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Long-term time series forecasting requires temporal dependency modeling that remains stable and generalizable under temporal distribution shifts. However, real-world time series are often noisy and non-stationary, making deep learning models prone to fitting incidental temporal interactions in the training data. A key question is whether there exist temporal relationship structures that recur across different temporal positions and variables. We analyze temporal relationship matrices on commonly used time series datasets and find that samples from different temporal positions and different variables exhibit shared dominant temporal relationship structures. This indicates that temporal relationship structures contain patterns that recur stably across samples and variables. To learn such shared structures, we propose \textbf{T}emporal \textbf{Struct}ure Network (\textbf{TStruct}), a simple yet effective network for directly learning shared and generalizable temporal dependencies. Specifically, TStruct directly parameterizes a set of shared temporal dependency matrices and generates normalized combination weights using dynamic sample information and static variable priors. These weights represent a soft allocation of each sample-variable pair over shared temporal dependency structures, enabling the model to generate adaptive temporal dependency matrices under shared structural constraints, rather than fitting incidental interactions in a fully unconstrained manner. Notably, this simple structure-aware design consistently outperforms several strong baselines across all datasets, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining high computational efficiency.

title: Nearly Optimal Quantum Sample Complexity of Learning Fourier-Sparse Boolean Functions
abstract: We study the number of uniform quantum examples needed to exactly learn a Boolean function with at most $k$ nonzero Fourier coefficients. We give a learner with near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(k)$ sample complexity independent of the input length $n$. The learner uses only separate measurements of individual examples. This improves the previous $O(k^{3/2}\log^2 k)$ upper bound (Arunachalam, Chakraborty, Lee, Paraashar, and de Wolf, 2021). The main ingredient is a candidate set formed by symmetric differences of subsets from independent groups of Fourier samples. A multilinear majority polynomial combines unbiased random approximations into an accurate witness whose Fourier support lies in this set. Granularity then forces the set to contain the entire Fourier support, including subsets never directly sampled. For comparison, we derive the tight classical sample complexity $Θ(nk)$ by combining known sparse-recovery and lower-bound results.

title: Explore with Memory, Learn without It: In-Context Exploration and Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
abstract: Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF

title: Confine to the Task, Anchor the Rest: Concept-Guided Retention Regularizer for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been widely used, yet the adapted model suffers catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. While most existing work hardens the adapter by constraining where the weight update may lie, we note that constraining this weight channel does not constrain the activation channel. In this paper, we propose Concept-Guided Retention (CGR), a plug-and-play regularizer that constrains both for any PEFT base. CGR reads a frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) and treats two disjoint concept sets differently. It softly confines the update to the task-concept subspace (via weight channel), and anchors a selected set of general-purpose concepts to the frozen model (via activation channel). We also provide anchor value bounds based on weight updates to understand how they interact, and show that both terms are necessary. On a CLIP vision panel, CGR significantly improves retention at comparable accuracy for every base, and the same pattern holds for world-knowledge retention under Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning. Because the protected directions are named SAE concepts, CGR remains inspectable and controllable.

evidence.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been widely used, yet the adapted model suffers catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. While most existing work hardens the adapter by constraining where the weight update may lie, we note that constraining this weight channel does not constrain the activation channel. In this paper, we propose Concept-Guided Retention (CGR), a plug-and-play regularizer that constrains both for any PEFT base. CGR reads a frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) and treats two disjoint concept sets differently. It softly confines the update to the task-concept subspace (via weight channel), and anchors a selected set of general-purpose concepts to the frozen model (via activation channel). We also provide anchor value bounds based on weight updates to understand how they interact, and show that both terms are necessary. On a CLIP vision panel, CGR significantly improves retention at comparable accuracy for every base, and the same pattern holds for world-knowledge retention under Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning. Because the protected directions are named SAE concepts, CGR remains inspectable and controllable.

title: CryoTracer: A Synthetic-to-Real System for Filament Instance Tracing in Cryo-EM
abstract: Particle picking in cryo-electron microscopy is commonly formulated as an object-detection problem in which individual particles are represented by bounding boxes, a natural representation for globular particles but a poor match for filaments that can extend across an entire micrograph. Existing methods reconstruct filament trajectories by linking local predictions in a separate post-processing stage, decoupling detection from instance formation and creating potential ambiguities at gaps and crossings. Directly preserving filament identity is particularly useful for polymorphic specimens, where segments originating from the same filament should remain associated. However, learning such instance-level representations is challenging because expert centerline annotations are scarce and costly to obtain. We introduce CryoTracer, a synthetic-to-real framework that addresses this limitation through procedural micrograph generation, transformer-based polyline prediction, and specimen-specific fine-tuning. Procedural pretraining exposes the model to diverse filament geometries, intersections, and imaging conditions before adaptation using a limited number of fully annotated experimental micrographs. CryoTracer represents filaments as ordered centerline polylines and optimizes their geometry using an orientation-invariant discrete Fréchet objective, enabling consistent learning regardless of tracing direction. Evaluation on established and newly expert-annotated datasets shows that CryoTracer improves instance-level filament recovery over existing particle-detection approaches. These results establish end-to-end polyline prediction as a practical alternative to detection-and-linking pipelines for recovering complete filament instances with limited micrograph annotation budgets. Code and data are available at https://github.com/cryotracer/cryotracer

title: Learning a Group Element from Its Action: Galois Correspondences, Optimal ERM, and an Abel-Ruffini Threshold for the Natarajan Dimension
abstract: We study learning an unknown element $g$ of a group acting with finite orbits on a countable set, from examples $(x,gx)$. After a sample on $A$, the consistent hypotheses are the restrictions of a coset of the pointwise stabilizer of $A$, and the sample forces exactly the labels of points this stabilizer fixes; for a Galois group, they form the field generated by the data. Through this correspondence, multiclass dimensions become group invariants: the DS and graph dimensions equal the height, the Littlestone dimension the longest irredundant sequence length, and the teaching dimension the minimal base size. Among deterministic learners, symmetry makes empirical risk minimization optimal: on nondegenerate classes every consistent learner, whatever its tie-breaking, attains the optimal realizable sample complexity up to constant factors, and every consistent online learner the optimal mistake bound. Agnostically, every ERM's sample complexity exceeds the known lower bound by at most the DS-to-Natarajan ratio, up to constants. For finite Galois extensions of countable fields, the Natarajan dimension equals a group invariant, the coset-cube number, which is at least the number of complemented factors of any chief series of any subgroup. Hence the dimensions coincide for every solvable Galois group, while for the groups $A_5$ and $S_5$ of the quintic they are $2<3$ and $3<4$, and $A_5$ is the smallest group with a gap. For the Galois group $S_n$ of the general equation of degree $n$, they coincide exactly when $n\le 4$, i.e., in characteristic zero, exactly when the equation is solvable by radicals; the implication is one-way, as the simple group $\mathrm{PSL}(2,8)$ has no gap. For linear, orthogonal and unitary maps of $\mathbb R^d$ or $\mathbb C^d$ both dimensions equal $d$, and a two-fibered pseudo-cube is a disjoint union of Natarajan cubes exactly when its monodromy group is abelian.

title: JANUBIY O'ZBEKISTONDA QO'RG'OSHIN–RUH MA'DANLASHUVINING G'ILON HUDUDIGA XOS FORMATSION TIPLARI: GEOLOGIK-GENETIK XUSUSIYATLARI VA PROGNOZ-QIDIRUV MEZONLARI
abstract: Maqolada Janubiy O'zbekistonning Hisor tog'lari doirasida joylashgan G'ilon istiqbolli maydonida qo'rg'oshin–ruh va kompleks polimetall ma'danlashuvini prognozlashning geologik-genetik asoslari tahlil qilindi. Rasmiy ma'lumotlarda G'ilon maydoni mis, ruh va qo'rg'oshin bo'yicha istiqbolli obyekt sifatida qayd etilgan. Janubi-g'arbiy Hisordagi Xondiza kabi yaxshi o'rganilgan kolchedan-polimetall tizimlar analog sifatida ko'rib chiqildi, biroq ularning G'ilonga to'liq tenglashtirilishi emas, balki qidiruv mezonlarini shakllantirishdagi metodik ahamiyati asoslandi. Litologik-stratigrafik, struktur-tektonik, magmatik, gidrotermal-metasomatik, mineralogik va geokimyoviy belgilarni birgalikda baholash asosida istiqbolli uchastkalarni reytinglash sxemasi taklif etildi. Pb–Zn–Cu–Ag assotsiatsiyalari, sfalerit–galenit–pirit–xalkopirit mineral majmuasi, uzilmalar kesishgan zonalar va gidrotermal o'zgarishlar asosiy qidiruv indikatorlari sifatida ajratildi.

title: A Three-Layer Architecture for Human-Interpretable Machine Reasoning.
abstract: Abstract Modern AI solvers can generate correct solutions to complex problems, yet their internal reasoning remains inaccessible to human decision‑makers. This document proposes a modular architecture designed to make advanced machine reasoning transparent and interpretable. The system consists of three coordinated layers: a Solver, which performs high‑speed reasoning; a Trace System, which reconstructs the solver’s full reasoning path into a structured map; and an Interpreter, which translates that map into human‑understandable concepts, narratives, and implications. While solver systems already exist in early form, the trace and interpreter layers remain undeveloped. This proposal outlines the missing components required to build an integrated, human‑interpretable reasoning pipeline and establishes a foundation for future research, collaboration, and development.

title: Evaluación de arquitecturas RAG descentralizadas para la reducción de alucinaciones y mejora de la trazabilidad en entornos corporativos simulados
abstract: La incorporación de modelos de lenguaje de gran escala en entornos organizacionales requiere mecanismos que permitan mejorar la recuperación de información y reducir la generación de respuestas no sustentadas en fuentes verificables. El objetivo del estudio fue evaluar una arquitectura de generación aumentada por recuperación (Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG) descentralizada orientada a mejorar la trazabilidad de la información y reducir las alucinaciones en entornos corporativos simulados. Se implementó un entorno experimental basado en un corpus sintético de 10000 documentos corporativos distribuidos en repositorios vectoriales federados. La arquitectura propuesta integró cuatro componentes principales: ingesta distribuida, almacenamiento vectorial federado, enrutamiento semántico y mecanismos de validación de respuestas mediante guardrails. Se evaluaron escenarios comparativos entre arquitecturas centralizadas y descentralizadas utilizando métricas de tiempo hasta el primer token (TTFT), tasa de alucinación, fidelidad de respuesta mediante RAGAS y validación humana. Los resultados evidenciaron una reducción del TTFT desde 3,2 s hasta 0,4 s en consultas complejas y una disminución de la tasa de alucinación desde 32,0 % hasta 1,9 % en el entorno experimental evaluado. Asimismo, la validación humana mostró una concordancia sustancial en la identificación de respuestas alucinadas (Kappa de Fleiss = 0,82). Se concluye que las arquitecturas RAG descentralizadas contribuyeron a mejorar la eficiencia de recuperación y la trazabilidad de las respuestas generadas en entornos corporativos simulados. No obstante, se requieren estudios adicionales para validar estos resultados en escenarios organizacionales reales.

title: Gaussian approximation for linear stochastic approximation with an application to reinforcement learning
abstract: Рассматривается задача статистического вывода для решения системы линейных уравнений A ¯ θ ⋆ = b ¯ , в которой матрица A и вектор b неизвестны, а вместо них доступны зашумлённые наблюдения. Исследуется метод линейной стохастической аппроксимации с постоянным шагом и марковским шумом. Усреднение Поляка–Рупперта (PR) снижает дисперсию, но сохраняет стационарное смещение порядка α , ухудшающее нормальную аппроксимацию. Для устранения ведущего смещения используется экстраполяция Ричардсона–Ромберга: средние двух рекурсий с шагами α и 2 α , использующих одну и ту же траекторию марковской цепи, объединяются в одну оценку. Показано, что такая коррекция улучшает нормальную аппроксимацию без изменения предельной дисперсии. Получена неасимптотическая оценка в расстоянии Колмогорова для скалярных проекций PR-усреднений с экстраполяцией Ричардсона–Ромберга. Для траектории длины n при выборе шага порядка n − 1 / 2 полученная верхняя граница убывает как n − 1 / 4 с точностью до логарифмических множителей. В качестве приложения исследуемой теории рассматривается построение доверительных интервалов для параметров, оцениваемых алгоритмом TD(0) в обучении с подкреплением. Численные эксперименты на синтетических данных подтверждают коррекцию среднего и улучшение покрытия доверительных интервалов без заметного увеличения их ширины.

title: AIRIME: a scalable adaptive RIME algorithm for feature optimization and data-driven monkeypox disease prediction
abstract: The rapid growth of big data in recent applications has created a pressing need for scalable and efficient optimization algorithms capable of handling large-scale and high-dimensional problems. Addressing this challenge, an Adaptive Improved Rime-Ice Optimization algorithm (AIRIME) is proposed which is built on the physics-based RIME algorithm inspired by the formation of soft and hard rime on surfaces. While RIME offers a strong theoretical foundation, it is hindered by limited exploratory capability, slow convergence, and an imbalance between exploration and exploitation. AIRIME introduces four key enhancements, including Adaptive k-Average-Best Mutation (AKAB), Adaptive Searching Process (ASP), Enhanced Solution Quality (ESQ), and Gaussian-Based Optimal Solution Mutation (GBOM), to overcome these challenges and meet the requirements of big data applications. AIRIME was rigorously tested on 41 functions from the CEC2017 and CEC2022 test suites, outperforming various classical, recent and advanced algorithms. Statistical evaluations, including Friedman rank and Wilcoxon rank tests, validated its superior performance and robustness. Sensitivity analyses further demonstrated the adaptability and efficiency of the proposed strategies. Moreover, a binary version of AIRIME was applied to feature selection (FS) tasks across 14 datasets, achieving promising results compared to various established binary metaheuristics. Furthermore, its real-world applicability was demonstrated in a novel Monkeypox disease prediction framework, where AIRIME helped to achieve an exceptional classification accuracy of 95.52% while selecting significantly fewer features, underscoring its efficiency in classifying high-dimensional healthcare data. Thus, AIRIME represents a significant advancement in big data-driven optimization, combining scalability, adaptability, and robustness to address complex and high-dimensional challenges across various domains, including critical healthcare applications.

title: Adaptive Computation with Conformal Certification
abstract: Scientific imaging data involving medical (e.g., 3D radiographic, microscopic images) and astronomical sensors pose different challenges from natural images. One key challenge is that these datasets are often orders of magnitude larger than natural images. Efficient training and inference on such data is challenging due to the increased hardware requirements, often needing bespoke solutions. Moreover, the relevant objects such as tumors and astronomical phenomena are sparsely distributed with respect to the background information. Standard efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning apply uniform scaling of all regions, potentially compromising the precision/fidelity of predictions. Thus, efficient methods that reduce computational requirements without losing resolution for relevant parts of the data and with uncertainty estimates on predictions are essential. We present \textit{Conformal Adaptation} with risk guarantees for uncertainty-aware sparse computations. evidence.abstract: Scientific imaging data involving medical (e.g., 3D radiographic, microscopic images) and astronomical sensors pose different challenges from natural images. One key challenge is that these datasets are often orders of magnitude larger than natural images. Efficient training and inference on such data is challenging due to the increased hardware requirements, often needing bespoke solutions. Moreover, the relevant objects such as tumors and astronomical phenomena are sparsely distributed with respect to the background information. Standard efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning apply uniform scaling of all regions, potentially compromising the precision/fidelity of predictions. Thus, efficient methods that reduce computational requirements without losing resolution for relevant parts of the data and with uncertainty estimates on predictions are essential. We present \textit{Conformal Adaptation} with risk guarantees for uncertainty-aware sparse computations. Our formalism is general, spanning dense pixel-level classification and regression tasks where hierarchical models predict at low resolution, certify the signal using conformal risk control, and refine the certified predictions. title: RepProbe: Can Video Language Models Count Repeated Actions? A Diagnostic Benchmark
abstract: Repetition counting requires identifying and enumerating action cycles over time. While state-of-the-art video language models describe actions fluently, they fail to reliably count how many times an action repeats. To investigate this limitation, we introduce RepProbe, a benchmark of 42K real and synthetic video clips containing exactly k in [1, 20] complete repetitions, with controls for clip position, temporal coverage, and duration. These controls allow us to study the counting failure directly and locate where in the model it arises. Counting accuracy collapses at high counts across the video language models we evaluate, and controlled experiments show this collapse is not explained by frame sampling alone. We compare model outputs with linear probes trained on the final-layer representations used to generate those outputs. We find a consistent representation-to-output dissociation: substantial count information remains linearly decodable even when models fail to report the correct count. Further analysis shows this failure arises primarily at the output stage, where answers concentrate on a small set of preferred numbers rather than the available count information. The dissociation holds on both real and synthetic videos and is not explained by clip duration, position, or scene content. These results indicate that models encode repetition structure but do not reliably report it in their outputs. Project page: https://arenaa.github.io/RepProbe-webpage/

title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Dissecting Clinical Evidence Acquisition in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often diagnose full sight, static clinical cases well yet struggle in foresight, dynamic diagnosis. Prior work has improved this limitation by quantifying the information models acquire and by developing stronger follow-up strategies to improve diagnostic accuracy. In contrast, we introduce a distinctive hindsight to systematically dissect why LLMs fail to acquire diagnostically critical evidence, tracing the failure from evidence identification, utilization and downstream diagnostic updating through not only diagnostic accuracy, but also evidence coverage, trajectory dynamics, and elicited probability and information entropy. Starting experiments from the breakdown at the level of capabilities, to the diagnosis of the pre-event state before the evidence arrives, and to the post-event state transition after the evidence arrives, our research has revealed the profound limitations and internal causes existing in the dynamic diagnostic process. At the same time, we have also conducted sufficient verification and generalization experiments to prove that these limitations are widespread. Together, these findings shift the central challenge from whether LLMs possess relevant clinical knowledge to whether they can identify, acquire, and effectively use the right evidence under clinical diagnosis and conduct a more detailed mechanism analysis to identify the exact location of the capability gap.
