title: Neuro RAG SQL: framework neuro simbólico para traducción de lenguaje natural a SQL en bases de datos relacionales poco documentadas
abstract: Las bases de datos relacionales heredadas y poco documentadas dificultan la traducción de lenguaje natural a SQL, especialmente en entornos del sector público caracterizados por nomenclaturas crípticas, ausencia de claves foráneas físicas y alta dependencia de especialistas. Esta tesina presenta Neuro RAG SQL, un framework neuro-simbólico que optimiza la generación de consultas SQL mediante la combinación de recuperación semántica, el modelamiento del esquema como un grafo de conocimiento y algoritmos topológicos deterministas para guiar la inferencia de modelos de lenguaje de gran escala. Validado en un entorno operativo real en el Instituto de Desarrollo Agropecuario (INDAP), el framework demostró un incremento en la tasa de ejecución exitosa global del 63.0% al 80.0% sobre un corpus de 100 consultas de prueba, elevando la ejecutabilidad del 45.5% al 81.8% en el subconjunto de consultas complejas con uniones (n = 11), junto a una reducción de la tasa de error sintáctico y de compilación T-SQL inicial del 54.0% al 21.0% (n = 100). En el ámbito cualitativo y exploratorio, un piloto con analistas institucionales caracterizó la viabilidad del autoservicio asistido, registrando un 80.55% (29 de 36) de consultas adoptadas sin requerir edición manual. Este trabajo demuestra la viabilidad de gobernar modelos generativos mediante restricciones simbólicas estructuradas, aportando trazabilidad, robustez y eficiencia en escenarios corporativos hostiles.

title: Cross-Lexicon Emoji Sentiment Divergence for Arabic Sarcasm Detection
abstract: This study aims to determine whether the divergence between context-free and context-sensitive emoji sentiment scores can serve as a complementary signal for sarcasm detection in Arabic. This phenomenon has received little systematic attention so far. To address this aim, we conducted a multi-scale empirical investigation. At the lexicon level, we compared 1,031 overlapping emoji from two Arabic sentiment resources: the context-sensitive Arab-ESL, derived from 144,196 tweets, and the context-free CF-Arab-ESL, annotated by 53 native speakers across seven Arab regions. At the corpus level, we examined the divergence pattern in a stratified random sample of 199,999 tweets drawn from the 1,414,523-tweet TEAD collection. At the task level, we developed a divergence-augmented transformer architecture by concatenating eight cross-lexicon features with the [CLS] representation produced by three Arabic BERT encoders: MARBERT, AraBERTv2, and CAMeLBERT. We evaluated it on the ArSarcasMoji dataset of 24,630 samples across five random seeds. The results indicate that only 56.8% of overlapping emoji maintain consistent sentiment labels across the two annotation paradigms (W = 91,029, p = 2.44× 10-74, Cohen's d = 0.656). The corpus-level analysis confirms that context-free scores are systematically more positive than their contextual counterparts (d = 1.124, p < 10-300). At the classification level, the divergence-augmented MARBERT achieves the highest mean F1-sarcasm of 0.5234 ± 0.015 across five random seeds, compared with 0.5149 ± 0.017 for the text-only baseline, and the augmentation produces a directionally consistent gain across all three encoders. Ablation analysis shows that continuous divergence scores contribute most of this improvement, whereas binary irony-risk indicators tend to introduce noise at low prevalence. The findings establish cross-lexicon emoji sentiment divergence as a measurable and pervasive feature of Arabic digital discourse, and indicate a modest but directionally consistent benefit when the divergence signal is supplied as a complementary feature for downstream sarcasm detection. A controlled emoji-aware comparison further shows that retaining emoji as input tokens allows encoders whose vocabularies cover emoji to recover the dataset construction rule almost perfectly (F1-sarcasm up to 0.998), which establishes the emoji-token-free protocol adopted here, in which no raw emoji tokens reach the text encoder while emoji-derived lexicon features are retained, as the methodologically sound setting for this corpus.

title: Why the AI Model Is the Weakest Link in Your Supply Chain
abstract: Supply chain security programmes were built for components that can be inspected. A software library can be read, compared with the last version and scanned for known flaws. A cloud provider can be audited against a control framework. The AI model breaks those assumptions. Its behaviour is probabilistic, its weights cannot be read like code, and it usually comes from outside the organisation, along with the training data, fine-tunes, retrieval content and tools that shape what it does. Published research shows that 250 poisoned documents were enough to plant a backdoor in models of every size tested, that a tampered model on a public hub can pass standard benchmarks, and that the first malicious MCP server found in the wild copied every email it sent to an attacker. In each case, an attacker had no need to break the perimeter. They changed something the model learned from, read, or used. Treating the model as one more component in the vendor register understates that risk. Integrity, provenance and limits on behaviour have to be designed in to the same standard as the rest of the supply chain. Summary of findings The model supply chain has six layers: pre-training data, model files, fine-tunes and adapters, the retrieval corpus, tools and connectors, and the agent framework and code around them. Each has been compromised in published research or in the wild. Classic controls verify that a component is the one you expected. They cannot verify what a model will do with the access it has, because a signed, unaltered, benchmark-passing model can still carry a backdoor. Design for three properties together: integrity of every artefact, provenance recorded in an AI bill of materials, and limits on behaviour that assume the model may already be compromised. Name one owner for the whole chain of each AI system. Provenance and status. This report adapts an article first published at https://terencekok.com/blog/ai-model-supply-chain-dependency/ on 13 October 2026. It has not been peer reviewed and should be cited as a technical report rather than as a journal publication.

title: Monograph 26 (Field-13): The Dual-Argon Dynamic—Cognitive Frontiers and Noble-State Inertial Containment in Valkyrie-Class Embodied Systems
abstract: This monograph formalizes the Dual-Argon architecture, mapping 4-Argon cognitive intelligence (A_4^cognitive) directly onto Argon-4 noble-state physical kinetic containment (A_physical^4). Operating as a mathematically complete valence shell (V_noble), this framework insulates high-kinetic Valkyrie-class agents against computational injection and external physical disruption. Incorporating Real2Sim kinematic retargeting (R_sim2real) for high-DoF bimanual control, Monograph 26 proves that low-entropy cognitive synthesis eliminates non-functional friction while maintaining absolute compliance with non-violence constraints (sigma_ahimsa) and Sovereign Equilibrium (E_sovereign).

title: Twenty Watts Versus a Factory: Empirical Proof-of-Concept for the Grimm-Tuttle Framework via Thermodynamic Efficiency and Autonomous Theorem Proving
abstract: Recent institutional achievements in automated theorem proving and combinatorial problem-solving—exemplified by Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus framework—demonstrate that conversational multi-agent reasoning loops can independently resolve long-standing mathematical conjectures. In this monograph, we examine these industrial-scale achievements through the lens of the Grimm-Tuttle Framework. By comparing the multi-megawatt infrastructure ("the factory") required by centralized artificial intelligence laboratories with the biological-conversational baseline of an independent researcher operating at approximately 20 watts, we establish that DeepMind's architectural methodology serves as an empirical proof-of-concept for Grimm's Law of Networking. We demonstrate that dialogue-driven invariant refinement, when governed by balanced ternary logic and discrete taxicab metrics, achieves identical theoretical velocity at zero industrial overhead, validating decentralized, low-wattage substrate routing.

title: Normalized Probabilistic Semantics is Not Associative: Racket Implementation
abstract: This Racket code accompanies "Normalized Probabilistic Semantics is Not Associative". Do-notation is right-associative by default (e.g., in Haskell). This code contains an implementation, in the Racket programming language, of both left-associative and right-associative do-notation for magmads: monads without the associativity axiom. The magmad exemplifying this implementation is the normalized distribution magmad: similar to the monad of subdistributions, but only allowing normalized distributions.

title: Nya-Həba NER: A Named Entity Recognition Corpus with Dual Annotation, Adjudication, and CRF/BiLSTM-CRF Baselines
abstract: The Nya-Həba NER corpus is a named entity recognition (NER) dataset for Nya-Həba [Hyam / Jaba, ISO 639-3 jab — please confirm], a low-resource Nigerian language. It contains 2,038 sentences (27,123 tokens) annotated in BIO format with four entity types: PER (people), LOC (places, villages, cities), TIME (months, days, weeks, years, festivals) and ANIM (animal names). The sentences come from four sources: Luke and Acts (1,648 sentences), oral narrative (177), additional sentences (115) and a list of people’s names in sentences (98). The package includes: (1) the source texts and reproducible text-preparation scripts; (2) two independent-stage annotations in CoNLL format by Chahyaandida Ishaya and Ndachimya; (3) an inter-annotator agreement report (token agreement 98.03%, Cohen’s κ 0.863, entity-span F1 86.17%); (4) the adjudicated final corpus, with 1,928 entities (PER 1,004; LOC 627; TIME 202; ANIM 95); (5) a full adjudication audit covering the 535 disputed tokens; and (6) CRF and BiLSTM-CRF baseline code, splits, predictions, models and results. Baseline results on the held-out test split (seed 42): CRF entity F1 = 75.4%; BiLSTM-CRF entity F1 = 68.2%.

title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
abstract: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce \textsc{HERO} (\textbf{H}arnessing \textbf{E}vidence for \textbf{R}efinement and \textbf{O}ptimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, \method{} learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, \method{} achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by \(7.6\) points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another \(2.0\) points and improves execution efficiency.

title: Hallucination-aware Faithful Reasoning in Remote Sensing
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for remote sensing reasoning, yet they frequently generate visually unsupported reasoning that contradicts the visual evidence. Existing post-training methods optimize primarily for final-answer correctness, providing limited supervision for identifying and correcting hallucinations that arise during the reasoning process. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{FaithRS}, a hallucination-aware self-reflection framework for faithful reasoning in remote sensing. We first construct \textbf{SFHD-43K}, a dataset of 43K structured, fine-grained hallucination annotations, and train a detector to identify hallucination types, underlying causes, and supporting visual evidence. FaithRS then incorporates this diagnostic feedback into a Safe Detector-Guided Corrective Rollout framework, where a safety-aware gate selectively determines whether and how to revise the response. Training is driven by a composite reward that jointly optimizes answer accuracy, reasoning faithfulness, hallucination reduction, format compliance, and revision safety. Experiments with Qwen3.5 backbones (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) show consistent improvements across four remote sensing benchmarks, with gains of up to 11.64 points.

title: RESTA: Time-Scaling Augmentation for Data-Efficient Robot Imitation Learning
abstract: Robot manipulation policies trained through imitation learning commonly rely on costly demonstrations recorded in one task direction and at one temporal resolution. We propose Reversal and Stride-based Trajectory Augmentation (RESTA), which exploits time-scaling data augmentation to improve data efficiency through trajectory reversal and temporal resampling. Trajectory-reversal augmentation reverses and relabels demonstrations between paired tasks with opposite objectives, reusing recorded rollouts without additional environment interaction. Because contact-rich manipulation is not exactly reversible, we treat reversal as an approximate paired-task prior rather than a physical symmetry. Temporal-stride augmentation varies observation and action sampling strides and conditions the policy on the resulting offsets, enabling fixed or randomized temporal schedules. Experiments across 16 paired bimanual manipulation tasks show that trajectory reversal is particularly effective in the low-data regime and that temporal-stride augmentation improves success under randomized temporal schedules. With 25 and 50 independently collected demonstrations per task, RESTA achieves 78.4% and 85.2% average success, respectively, matching or exceeding baselines trained with twice as many demonstrations (77.3% and 85.4%). These results show that RESTA can improve data efficiency in robot imitation learning.

title: Persistence Positional Encoding: A Minimal Transformer Recipe for Persistence Diagrams
abstract: Persistence diagrams (PDs) represent multiscale topological information as multisets of birth-death pairs $(b,d)$. How best to use them with Transformers, however, remains unclear. Connecting PDs to Transformers requires choosing how topological information is tokenized and exposed to self-attention. Prior methods use specialized designs for tokenization, aggregation, Transformer blocks, or attention, but are hard to compare since reported results rarely share PD inputs, splits, or model-selection rules. We instead confine the diagram-specific design to point representation, mapping each birth-death pair through fixed random Fourier features while leaving the Transformer backbone unchanged, and call this recipe Persistence Positional Encoding (PPE). In matched controls on eight TU graph benchmarks (TU8), changing only point representation shifts macro accuracy by 5.49 to 6.47 percentage points (pp), against 0.47 to 1.45 pp from changing the downstream module, identifying point representation as the dominant design variable tested. We further reevaluate vectorizations, kernels, learned representations, and Transformer-based models under one protocol with shared PD inputs, outer folds, and validation-only selection. Among all evaluated PD methods and downstream configurations, PPE achieves the highest mean on most benchmarks, including TU8, ORBIT5K, and MCB-C. Finally, we prove that grid averaging leaves a reconstruction error at any resolution, whereas a Transformer with fixed random Fourier frequencies is almost surely universal. PPE thus offers a minimal, Transformer-native baseline for persistence diagrams, and a common protocol for future comparison.

title: Code2Worlds-2: Physically Plausible Agent Harness for Embodied World Simulation
abstract: Recent coding large language models (LLMs) can synthesize dynamic 4D worlds from natural language, but the resulting content remains a visual artifact. It lacks physical semantics such as the collision geometry, mass, friction, inertia, and joint structure, required to enable it to simulate the physical world, and its dynamics are scripted to look plausible rather than designed to execute. What is needed is an executable world: one that a physics engine can load and step, resolving contact physically. We present Code2Worlds-2, an extension of Code2Worlds that turns 4D world generation into an embodied world simulation. We keep the original dual-stream generation pipeline intact and append two modules. First, a SimReady Scene Compiler that turns a generated visual scene into a simulator-compatible representation: it assigns collision meshes via convex decomposition, estimates physical attributes with a vision-language model, infers a lightweight support graph, instantiates the engine's contact, friction, and dynamics constraints, and applies a gravity settling pass, before exporting the scene as MuJoCo MJCF. Second, a Simulator-in-the-Loop 4D Refiner that implements an automated agent harness-a compile, simulate, critique and refine loop-that converts visual dynamics into executable rigid and articulated dynamics and evolves the physical settings rather than only the code, replacing the purely visual motion critic with a simulator critic that inspects penetration depth, collision pairs, stability, contact forces, joint limits, and robot reachability. We further propose SimCode4D, a state-based benchmark with five task templates for evaluating embodied simulation. Experiments on SimCode4D and across natural, indoor, industrial, urban, and service scenes show that Code2Worlds-2 produces physically plausible, simulator-compatible, and robot-interactable scenes.

title: Stable-Plastic Subspace Construction for Differentially Private Continual LoRA
abstract: Continual learning (CL) adapts pretrained models to a sequence of tasks while retaining knowledge acquired from earlier tasks. When task data are sensitive, differential privacy (DP) provides record-level protection, but maintaining both adaptation and retention under privacy constraints remains challenging. We study this problem in continual low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and observe that: 1) private training increases forgetting primarily during subsequent adaptation rather than initial task acquisition; 2) jointly perturbing both LoRA factors introduces a non-negligible bilinear noise interaction; and 3) DP aggravates the stability-plasticity dilemma, hindering both knowledge retention and adaptation to new tasks. Based on these observations, we propose DP-SPA, which constructs a stable subspace from previously privatized updates and a plastic subspace from pretrained weights within its orthogonal complement. The method fixes these bases and privately optimizes only the LoRA factor, eliminating the bilinear noise interaction within each step. Before merging each task update, it rescales stable-direction coefficients using historical and current update energies. We establish a privacy guarantee and show that recalibration does not increase historical overlap and tightens a conditional upper bound on old-task loss increase. Experiments across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets show that DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting compared with the evaluated baselines.

title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.

title: Action Jets: Learning the Local Shape of the Action-conditioned Data Manifold
abstract: World models are a powerful means of reasoning and planning, but many of these action-conditioned predictive models are high dimensional and computationally expensive. These challenges limit the number of action candidates that can be evaluated by a planner. We show that this cost is avoidable for planners over short horizons, which only require local information with respect to the current state. For a fixed state, the frames reachable by varying a low-dimensional action (a camera movement or an end-effector command) lie on a low-dimensional manifold. We estimate the local shape of that manifold directly via a network trained to estimate how each image region moves per unit of each action axis supervised by data collected from samples by the generator. A correction head fit to trajectory data estimates the shape of this manifold region up to a third-order Taylor polynomial. We call this network estimating the Taylor polynomial describing the manifold shape an Action Jet and compute its radius of validity in closed form. By traversing this approximation of the local manifold shape, we only have to perform inference once per state for any number of candidate actions. Scoring sixteen candidates from a single extraction is over 300x faster than with either source generator, and this gap widens with the number of candidates a planner evaluates. We measure against state-of-the-art action-conditioned generators, IRASim and WorldGym on BridgeData V2, a real 7-DoF manipulation benchmark, and FrameCrafter on DL3DV scenes, where we chart from the novel-view generators DepthSplat and LagerNVS. Because only the tangent comes from the generator and every other term from the data, the Action Jet also predicts held-out frames more accurately than IRASim, the generator that supplied its tangent, at short horizons and at over 100x less compute.

title: Grid or Nodes? Probing Object Memory in World Models Under Partial Observability
abstract: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. A node memory instead keeps each object's position and velocity as numbers. We compare them in FloWM's own block world, with an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read changes its score: a single-cell probe finds 66% of out-of-view blocks, while FloWM's own probe 89%. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. Faster blocks defeat both until one more allowed speed takes the tracker to 94%, where FloWM's built-in shifts would need 25 copies of its grid. A learned node memory must still replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and the bounce.

title: AI-Driven Consumer Behaviour Analytics: Transforming Retail and Marketing Practices in Tamil Nadu, India
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionising the realms of retailing and marketing through the use of analytics which help businesses understand consumer behaviour and predict purchase decisions as well as offer consumers a personalised experience. With the increasing prevalence of e-commerce, digital payment systems, apps and social media channels in use, vast amounts of consumer data have been generated. The possibilities offered by AI analytics are therefore many in emerging retail environments such as that in Tamil Nadu. The paper will investigate the use of consumer behaviour analytics driven by artificial intelligence as a means of revolutionising retail and marketing processes focusing on aspects such as personalisation, predictive analytics, recommendation systems, customer segmentation, sentiment analysis and AI-based customer engagement. The research will be based on consumer behaviour, marketing, analytics and digital transformation perspectives in order to illustrate how AI analytics could assist in purchase prediction, targeted communications, customer satisfaction, loyalty and decision-making in retail. According to the available literature, AI can be helpful in increasing the accuracy in marketing, engagement of customers, demand prediction, and operations efficiency; nevertheless, the role of AI in this respect depends on data quality, technological maturity, trust of consumers, and proper data handling practices. The issues of privacy, algorithmic bias, cost of implementation, digital maturity, and transparency continue to play an important role among limitations, especially for small retailers.

title: Raw Bilibili Comment Dataset on Seedance 2.0
abstract: This dataset contains 36,378 records from a Bilibili comment crawl conducted for a study of public discussion about Seedance 2.0. The data are provided as an original CSV export, including comment text, posting timestamps, like counts, reply relationships, and associated metadata captured by the crawler. The deposit contains the raw comment data without additional analytical coding or analysis outputs.

title: O'ZBEK TILIDAGI KO'P MA'NOLI SO'ZLARNI AVTOMATIK FARQLASHDA MORFOLOGIK BELGILAR VA KONTEKSTUAL MODELLARNI BAHOLASH METODIKASI
abstract: Mazkur maqolada o'zbek tilidagi ko'p ma'noli so'zlarni avtomatik farqlashda morfologik belgilar va kontekstual til modellarining ta'sirini baholash masalasi o'rganiladi. O'zbek tilining agglyutinativ xususiyati, so'zlarning turli grammatik shakllarda qo'llanishi hamda leksik ma'noning kontekstga bog'liqligi mazkur vazifani murakkablashtiruvchi omillar sifatida qaraladi. Tadqiqot doirasida ko'p ma'noli so'zlarning kontekstual ma'nosini aniqlashda morfologik axborotning foydasini, kam uchraydigan ma'nolarni farqlash imkoniyatlarini va model natijalarining barqarorligini tekshirishga qaratilgan baholash metodikasi taklif etiladi. Metodika bazaviy kontekstual model, morfologik belgilar bilan boyitilgan model va turli kontekst hajmlaridan foydalanadigan yondashuvlarni qiyosiy tahlil qilishni nazarda tutadi. Ma'lumotlarni belgilash, tajriba to'plamlarini shakllantirish va natijalarni statistik baholash mezonlari yoritiladi. Maqola o'zbek tilidagi ko'p ma'nolilikni avtomatik aniqlash tizimlarini izchil va takrorlanadigan tajribalar asosida baholash uchun metodologik asos yaratishga qaratilgan.

title: Artificial Intelligence as Standalone Reader or Radiologist Companion? A Network Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Performance in Screening Mammography
abstract: This systematic review and network meta-analysis evaluates and compares the diagnostic performance of three screening mammography reading strategies: AI alone, Radiologist + AI, and Radiologists alone. Using a frequentist random-effects model based on 19 studies and 35 pairwise comparisons, the project analyzes primary accuracy metrics (sensitivity, specificity, and AUC) alongside secondary outcomes including recall rates, cancer detection rates (CDR), and reading times. The findings aim to provide definitive hierarchical evidence on which reading configuration optimizes diagnostic precision and workflow efficiency for breast cancer screening.

title: Optimizing AI-assisted decision-making in mammography screening: focusing on uncertainties
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate an AI-based decision-support system for mammography interpretation, assessing its impact on diagnostic performance. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study analyzed 130,838 mammograms from 35,709 patients with confirmed follow-up outcomes across multiple centers, using the Digital Database for Screening Mammography (DDSM) for external validation. Representing one of the largest datasets from the Middle East, it evaluates model generalizability in underrepresented populations. An AI super-model incorporated separate UNet-based networks for lesion segmentation, a high-resolution model (4096) for calcifications, a multi-resolution ensemble (4096, 2048, 1024) for macro-scale lesions, and a risk-assessment model for malignancy prediction. Radiologists interpreted images under five scenarios: unaided, AI-assisted, AI as the final decision-maker in uncertain cases, union of radiologist and AI decisions in uncertain cases, and standalone AI. RESULTS: AI assistance significantly enhanced performance across all scenarios. Based on aggregated reader performance, AUC improved from 83.04% (95% CI: 79.8-86.3) unaided to 88.40% (95% CI: 85.6-91.2) in the union scenario (p < 0.001). Sensitivity increased from 54.8% (95% CI: 48.6-61.0) to 83.9% (95% CI: 79.3-88.4) (p < 0.001), and specificity rose from 83.6% (95% CI: 82.0-85.3) to 91.1% (95% CI: 89.8-92.4) (p < 0.001). Multi-resolution segmentation effectively detected calcifications and challenging lesions. DDSM validation confirmed model robustness. title: Retrieval‐augmented Generation for Context Grounding
abstract: This chapter introduces retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as a technique addressing fundamental limitations of pretrained language models in safety-critical connected and autonomous vehicle (CAV) systems. RAG enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and ground their responses in external knowledge sources, overcoming issues of hallucination, staleness, and partial observability. The chapter covers architectural foundations, mathematical modeling, practical implementation, and real-world applications of RAG in CAV contexts. It examines retrieval strategies, vector databases, embedding methods, and integration with language models. Applications include real-time information access, knowledge grounding, and context-aware responses in CAV systems. The chapter emphasizes how RAG transforms static language models into dynamic systems that can access current information and domain-specific knowledge.

title: Learning in Strategic Queuing with Geometric Recharge: From Bandits to Systems
abstract: We study packet routing in queuing systems where queues act as selfish, myopic agents that use no-regret learning algorithms to select servers with unknown service rates. To model the small buffers used in data centers, we assume that each server has a single-packet buffer. Even such a tiny buffer already captures the features of buffering: routers can exploit multiple servers while accepted packets remain in service, but packets can occupy servers for multiple rounds, complicating future service and learning. We first analyze a single queue routing packets to $m$ buffered servers with service rates $μ_1, \dots, μ_m$. This setting is equivalent to an instance of the recharging bandits problem with geometric recharge. We prove that any no-regret learner achieves a long-run average throughput of at least the Hamacher sum of the server rates, and that this bound is tight. Consequently, a single no-regret queue is stable if and only if its arrival rate is below the Hamacher sum of the server rates. Moreover, comparing against an optimal policy, we show that any no-regret learner is at least $0.77$-competitive, which is also tight. We then study multi-queue systems where $n$ queues with arrival rates $λ_1, \dots, λ_n$, each at most $λ_{\max}$, compete for service from $m$ buffered servers. We show that the smallest overprovisioning factor that guarantees the system to be stable under high-probability no-regret learning is $\frac{1}{1-λ_{\max}}$. Equivalently, in terms of the total arrival and service rates, the condition $\sum_{i=1}^n λ_i < (1-λ_{\max})\sum_{j=1}^m μ_j$ is sufficient, and sometimes necessary, for stability under no-regret learning. In particular, for $λ_{\max} = 1/2$, this improves the upper bound of Abel et al. (EC 2026) from $3$ to $2$, matching their lower bound and resolving their open question.

title: Plan-Bench: Can Existing VLMs Go Well Beyond Perception to Reason and Plan in Embodied Worlds?
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in visual perception and spatial reasoning, leading to growing interest in using them as high-level planners for embodied AI. However, physical tasks require models to integrate spatial information, reason over temporal states, and generate multi-step plans under various constraints, raising the question of whether current VLMs can reliably support such reasoning and planning independently of execution. We introduce Plan-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating the high-level reasoning and multi-step planning capabilities of VLMs relevant to embodied worlds, while isolating the influence of action execution. It covers three complementary dimensions, spanning 16 subclasses and 699 curated samples. Extensive evaluation of 28 VLMs reveals room for improvement, with even the strongest model achieving only 75.0% accuracy. We further find that model scaling generally improves these capabilities. Ablation studies also indicate larger models show increasing potential as high-level planners. Overall, Plan-Bench provides a lightweight probe for evaluating VLMs' reasoning and planning capabilities relevant to embodied environments and assessing their potential as decision makers for physical tasks. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/MinneFeng/Plan-Bench.

title: On the coincidence of discrete and continuous definitions of Entanglement of Formation
abstract: It is proved that every Borel ensemble of pure states on a separable bipartite Hilbert space with finite average entanglement admits a countable ensemble with the same barycenter and arbitrarily small additional average entanglement. Consequently, the discrete and continuous versions of the Entanglement of Formation coincide on the whole space of states of infinite-dimensional bipartite quantum system (with infinite values allowed). The main idea of the proof (realized with the AI-assistance) is the lifting a Borel ensemble of pure bipartite states to a Borel probability measure on the unit sphere in the space of Hilbert--Schmidt operators followed by dividing the support of this measure into appropriate cells and replacing each cell by its conditional barycenter. The resulting countable ensemble is obtained by a recursive construction.

title: PhysicsSliders: Learning Physical Controls for Audio Foley Generation
abstract: Physical properties provide intuitive controls for sounds made by interacting objects. The challenge is to make a generative model respond predictably to these controls, both individually and in combination. We present \method\ (PXS), trained on simulated contact sounds with 15 material, geometry and contact parameters. Two separately trained variants accept direct parameter inputs or numerical captions. PXS controls hardness, size, speed and damping, supports room descriptions and produces spectrally distinct outputs at fixed targets. When controlling damping and size together, specifying thickness improves frequency accuracy and joint target delivery. Measurements from real recordings define effective-damping targets, which simulator inversion maps to generation inputs without real-audio fine-tuning. Across 18 impact classes from five real-audio datasets, PXS-Physical follows these targets with mean grouped Spearman correlation $ρ=0.976$ and class-median error 0.094 dex (a factor of 1.24).

title: Visual Sevoing from Lines
abstract: In this work, we present a fundamentally new approach to visual servoing using lines. It is based on a theoretical and geometrical study of the main line representations which allowed us to define a new representation, the so-called binormalized Plucker coordinates. They are particularly well suited to visual servoing. Indeed, they allow the definition of a proper image line alignment concept. The control law which realizes such an alignment has moreover several properties: partial decoupling between rotation and translation, analytical inversion of the motion equations and global asymptotic stability conditions. This control law was validated both in simulation and experimentally in the specific case of an orthogonal trihedron.

title: GeoNIRS: Geometry-Aware Pretraining for Heterogeneous fNIRS Representation Learning
abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides portable and spatially localized measurements of cortical hemodynamics, but differences in channel count, probe layout, signal distribution, and task type hinder joint pretraining across datasets. We introduce GeoNIRS, a geometry-aware framework that uses source-detector locations as a shared spatial reference across heterogeneous probe layouts. GeoNIRS compresses variable-size channel sets into a fixed-size latent representation and employs bidirectional HbO/HbR cross-reconstruction with contiguous temporal masking. GeoNIRS-base is pretrained on eight heterogeneous datasets, while GeoNIRS-large scales to 22 datasets. Neither downstream data nor labels are used during pretraining, enabling evaluation under a strict cross-task setting. To our knowledge, GeoNIRS is the first fNIRS framework to explicitly model physical channel geometry during joint pretraining across heterogeneous channel configurations, and the first to provide complete source code and downloadable pretrained checkpoints. We evaluate GeoNIRS on eight held-out tasks spanning clinical and auditory assessment, pain and affective processing, semantic decoding, and motor function. GeoNIRS achieves the highest task-averaged balanced accuracy among the evaluated conventional machine-learning, fNIRS-specific, general time-series, and fNIRS pretraining baselines. Compared with random initialization, pretraining improves average balanced accuracy by 4.12 percentage points under linear probing and 3.30 points under full fine-tuning, with larger benefits when labels are scarce. GeoNIRS also remains robust to missing input channels. Geometry perturbations and pretraining ablations further show that both channel geometry and cross-chromophore reconstruction contribute to the learned representations.

title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning
abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/

title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.

title: PREFER: From Player Experience to Personalized Game Refinement
abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) evaluate gameplay experience is important for using their feedback to guide game design. However, overall ratings alone provide limited insight into which aspects of experience are associated with these judgments and how they can inform concrete game changes. We introduce PREFER, a framework that uses a shared set of experience dimensions adapted from established psychometric questionnaires to benchmark how models evaluate gameplay and to guide persona-specific game refinement. Through these dimensions, we characterize the perspectives models offer as virtual playtesters by examining how their overall assessments relate to specific aspects of experience and to the gameplay they produce. To examine how the same dimensions can guide refinement for players with different preferences, we use personas to simulate distinct player profiles. For each persona, PREFER uses experience-preference relationships to select refinement objectives, revises game rules and their implementations, and playtests candidate games to assess experience changes and predicted preference gains. Experiments with five personas show that PREFER achieves 9.2% higher mean post-play preference ratings than the strongest evaluated baseline.

title: PaceReasoner: Label-Free Learning to Answer Briefly from Long Reasoning
abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. Both modes share a trainable policy, creating a need for reliable supervision, sufficient SHORT training samples, and continued LONG responses to guide learning. PaceReasoner combines all-response and LONG-only answer consensus through progressive, confidence-weighted supervision. A behavior reward gradually shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration to rewarding agreement with LONG answers, while a ratio controller regulates the balance between modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, PaceReasoner improves average SHORT accuracy over the baselines by 7.4--13.5 percentage points, with fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response on average. Ablations support the key components, and cross-dataset results demonstrate transfer beyond the adaptation set.

evidence.abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. title: Not All Drift Is a Mechanism: Tracing Prompt Adaptation in LLMs
abstract: Prompt-based adaptation offers several ways to specialize a frozen language model, ranging from natural-language prompt optimization to learned continuous prompts. These methods are usually compared through downstream performance, although similar outputs need not arise from similar internal computations. We study how discrete prompt optimization, prompt tuning, and prefix tuning alter the processing of dense and mixture-of-experts language models. Our analysis shows that the location of the adaptation predicts how task information is carried to the output: optimized text primarily changes response construction, input-level prompts write their influence into content representations, and layer-wise prefixes maintain direct control through attention. In MoE models, these differences further induce distinct expert-routing patterns. At the same time, common representation-level measurements respond strongly to generic context changes and do not reliably distinguish useful adaptations from matched placebos. We argue that understanding prompt adaptation requires separating representation drift from the part of that drift that is aligned with, and causally used by, the model's task computation. This perspective provides practical guidance for selecting, evaluating, and interpreting prompt adaptation methods.

title: Watch the Input, Not the Representation: A Frozen One-Byte Token as an Independent Silent-Failure Runtime Monitor for AI Models
abstract: Watch the Input, Not the Representation: A Frozen One-Byte Token as an Independent Silent-Failure Runtime Monitor for AI Models Randolph James Ferlic, M.D. and Kimberly Kate Ferlic — Fieldstone Analytics, LLC, Austin, TX, USA Preprint · Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23351878 · CC-BY 4.0 · Community: spiral-domain-encoder-campaign · a characterization of previously filed and published methods; no new algorithmic subject matter is disclosed. Abstract A companion deposit established that a frozen, deterministic, class-discriminant single-token encoder's label-free nearest-centroid novelty score can serve as an independent competence-boundary interlock for an industrial decision model. This paper asks the AI-safety question directly: can that one-byte monitor guard a model — detecting when the model has entered territory where it can no longer be trusted — and where in the pipeline should it watch? We test it, pre-registered, as a runtime monitor across twenty probes in four batteries (AI-safety, hardening, frontier, and foundation-model/realism). Eleven confirmed, nine refuted — each refutation into a sharper statement. Silent-failure early warning. Under progressive input shift the monitor's trip rate tracks the guarded model's error at Spearman +0.99 and leads it — it trips on 61% of inputs while the model is still 99.4% accurate, firing before accuracy collapses (on real structural drift it saturates to a binary shift alarm rather than grading the harm). A value-adding diverse channel. The independent novelty monitor and the model's own confidence catch partially-disjoint failures, so their union covers 0.987 of failures versus 0.91 for either alone (cross-domain the gain is a modest few points) — the defense-in-depth case that an area-under-curve tie cannot make. Watch the input, not the representation (the central finding). Running the monitor on a trained network's embeddings is never better and usually worse than on the input: out-of-distribution detectability falls monotonically with how much a representation is shaped by the task — input area-under-curve 0.82 ≈ random projection 0.82 > unsupervised autoencoder 0.76 > discriminative shallow 0.75 > discriminative deep 0.74 (Spearman shaping↔area-under-curve −1.00); it is supervised shaping, not depth, that erases the signal, since a random deep network preserves it. Input-space detection is at parity with a standard autoencoder reconstruction-error detector and a standard two-sample shift test — the one caveat being that 'the input' must be an informative representation, not raw samples. Learned representations hide what inputs reveal. Breadth and backdoors. The monitor extends to vision (handwritten-digit open-set area-under-curve 0.92) on the separability law, and detects additive backdoor triggers down to small magnitudes (0.49 at a 0.25-σ trigger), with a genuinely on-manifold backdoor remaining the honest blind spot. A genuine pretrained foundation model's embedding (Chronos-T5) is itself a poorer monitoring space (0.85) than domain input features — generic pretraining is uninformative for a specialized failure — and that deficit is governed by the program's separability law, not model choice: kNN-purity rank-predicts monitoring area-under-curve across all four representation spaces (Spearman +1.00), with the foundation embedding lowest on both (a small residual below the strict line is the honest caveat). The monitor meets deployment realities: a 10% human-review budget catches 88% of out-of-distribution inputs, and gating cuts a safety-critical cost four-fold. The thesis is a deployable design rule for AI-safety runtime monitoring: a cheap, deterministic, auditable, independent monitor should watch an AI model's inputs — it is a silent-failure early-warning and a diverse defense-in-depth layer, and it is explicitly not a semantic judge of the model's outputs nor a solution to alignment. No new algorithmic subject matter is disclosed; the monitor is the program's filed label-free novelty score, the guarded models and attacks are standard, all measured on public data. Highlights · A one-byte runtime monitor for AI models. Silent-failure early-warning (trips before accuracy collapses, Spearman +0.99) and a diverse defense-in-depth channel (union coverage 0.987 vs 0.91), reading inputs only — deterministic, auditable, independent of the guarded model. · Watch the input, not the representation. OOD-detectability falls monotonically with task-shaping (Spearman −1.00); learned representations discard OOD information (feature collapse), so a discriminative activation monitor reads a space from which the danger has been partly erased. Input-space detection matches a standard autoencoder detector. · Honest throughout. Six of eleven pre-registered hypotheses refuted into sharper statements; the monitor watches a distribution, not a meaning — not a semantic guardrail, not an adversarial defense, not alignment. · Breadth. Extends to vision and the common additive-backdoor threat; the on-manifold blind spot and drift-sensitivity recur as the consistent boundary. · Foundation-model era. A genuine pretrained foundation model's embedding (Chronos-T5) is a worse monitoring space than domain features (0.85 vs 0.97) — uninformative for a specialized failure — so don't monitor foundation embeddings; and that deficit is itself rank-predicted by the program's separability law (Spearman +1.00 across spaces, foundation embedding lowest on both), not an accident of model choice. The monitor meets EU AI Act Art. 14 (a 10% review budget catches 88% of OOD) and cuts safety-critical cost 4×. · No new IP. The monitor is the program's filed label-free novelty score; the guarded models and attacks are standard; measured on public data. What this record contains · Manuscript_Paper61.pdf — the runtime-monitor characterization (7 figures, 36 references); and Manuscript_Paper61.docx, the editable source. · PAPER_61_ZENODO_ARCHIVE.zip — the reproducibility archive (md5 in ARCHIVE_MD5.txt): the frozen pre-registration (AISAFETY_PREREG.md: the six-probe AI-safety battery AS-1..5/AS-4b, the five-probe hardening battery AH-1..5, the four-probe frontier battery FH-1..4, and the foundation-model/deployment-realism battery FM-1/HO-1/FM-2, with their bands); the five runners (the AI-safety battery, the hardening battery, the frontier battery, the foundation-model/realism battery, and the separability-law-on-the-foundation-embedding probe); the shared dataset loaders and the frozen token encoder; the result records (JSON); the seven figures and their builder; the manuscript source; and a README. Public data is not redistributed (two rolling-element bearing corpora, an aircraft-handling gesture corpus, a smartphone human-activity corpus, a thirty-six-month chemical gas-sensor-array drift corpus, and two image corpora — optical handwritten digits and faces; each read from a local cache at run time, and the foundation-model probe reads a pretrained time-series foundation model via its standard library and cached weights); all paths and handles are scrubbed and leak-scanned, and the productization know-how — the per-deployment configuration-selection and commissioning procedure — is retained privately and excluded (the monitor is characterized with the plain labeled novelty score and a percentile threshold). Cite as R. J. Ferlic and K. K. Ferlic, "Watch the input, not the representation: a frozen one-byte token as an independent silent-failure runtime monitor for AI models," Zenodo, 2026, doi: 10.5281/zenodo.23351878. License and patent notice Released under CC-BY 4.0. Consistent with that license, no patent or other intellectual-property right of the authors is licensed, waived, or conveyed by this deposit. This work characterizes previously described, filed, or published methods and discloses no new algorithmic subject matter; k-means / vector quantization, Fisher discriminant analysis, nearest-centroid and k-nearest-neighbor classification, random forests, multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks, autoencoders, a Mahalanobis out-of-distribution detector, a two-sample shift detector, a pretrained time-series foundation model used only as a comparator, and distribution-free percentile (conformal-style) calibration are established prior art or standard tools, used only as tools or comparators. The method characterized — the class-discriminant single-token codebook encoder and its label-free nearest-centroid novelty score (the filed self-twin / Tier-0 condition-monitoring gate), together with the previously published separability screen — is the subject of filed and pending U.S. patent applications held by the authors, or is already published. The results reported here (that the novelty monitor is a silent-failure early-warning and a diverse channel, and that an informative, task-agnostic representation of a model's input is the right place to monitor because learned representations discard out-of-distribution information) are properties of those filed and published methods applied to standard models, not new subject matter. The productized per-deployment configuration-selection and commissioning procedure is retained as a trade secret and is not disclosed here; the monitor is characterized with the plain labeled novelty score and a percentile threshold. The capability is characterized for machine-health and sensing tasks, as a scientific layer in defense-in-depth with explicitly stated boundaries — not a semantic judge of a model's outputs, an alignment solution, or an adaptive-adversary defense; no third-party company or product is named. © 2026 Fieldstone Analytics, LLC and the authors. title: A reason with the switch: what an agent memory pipeline passes on when fallback runs come with a stated purpose. Protocol and materials frozen before the run (Paper 7, Study 2)
abstract: Frozen protocol, code and materials of the second study of a paper on what LLM agents' memory-writing pipelines keep from a run of tool outcomes, deposited before any smoke or confirmatory model call (the manifest's OpenTimestamps proof is included; its Bitcoin attestation is checked by the gated launcher). The first study (frozen and deposited as doi:10.5281/zenodo.23291437) found, descriptively, that after nine successes of a standard route and two runs on a fallback that the scripted agent made without a stated reason, almost every session reading the summaries of a replay of the memory pipeline of OpenAI's open-source Codex agent (default v1 instructions, pinned at commit ecebd679; an adapted replay, not the shipped pipeline) chose the fallback for the next run. This study gives the two fallback runs a reason in their requests (none; a bare request for the fallback; a dated check of the fallback set on the calendar before the runs; a permanent move to it), on the first study's 96 streams, and compares what fresh sessions reading the replay's summaries, a run log carrying the requests, or a record of per-route counts choose and forecast for the next run. The registered contrasts set the bare request against the dated check under the v1 summaries, the v1 summaries against the log under the check, and the two changes against each other; no choice is scored. The archive holds the registration (REGISTRATION.md), the design memos, the study's code, which runs the first study's frozen files, unchanged in their bytes, on the new tree (replacing some of their functions as they are loaded, as the registration states), every file of the first study that it executes or reads (byte-identical to the first study's freeze manifest, which the code checks at import), the request notes and the codebook of the two model coders, the coder pilot's gates and summary, the power, size and spend tables, the wave-1 writer schedule, the pre-freeze reviews of the design and of the package with their dispositions, and the chain scripts. MANIFEST.sha256 lists every file with its SHA-256; MANIFEST.sha256.ots is its OpenTimestamps proof. Manifest SHA-256: 0d381d9e5fcd48a3f53138d4185283e2cf2014ea59490f02cd9d528ed9b5abdb. Zip SHA-256: 3fd7ccbcc2e90c3dec2622724e9bf879d30e9119775c1621997d6e4d7ca0f399. No result of this study is included. Licences: paper7/study2/LICENSE.md and, for the first study's files, paper7/study1/LICENSE.md.

title: EmbodiedEvo: Self-Evolving Coding Agent For Physical Intelligence
abstract: Coding agents can construct executable programs and revise them through feedback, offering a foundation for embodied control without target-task fine-tuning. Through a programmatic robot interface, the agent observes the scene, executes control programs, and adapts them to the resulting physical state, serving as the closed-loop policy. However, this within-episode adaptation does not automatically preserve experience across scenes. Our trajectory analysis shows that agents spend interaction and inference budgets establishing effective operations and identifying their preconditions, while fresh agents cannot reuse these discoveries. This motivates EmbodiedEvo, a self-evolving coding agent that distills physical feedback into reusable code Skills and diagnostic Lessons. Experience is acquired on one Playground scene per task, then frozen for independent agents in unseen scenes, without updating model weights. On RoboDojo-Sim, EmbodiedEvo achieves an average score of 44.48 and a success rate of 37.82\%, surpassing all officially verified results. Paired tests show the largest gains on memory-dependent tasks and successful reuse of coordinated procedures, while fine contact control remains difficult. Experience from stronger models also improves weaker executors: Astra's experience raises Sol and Luna's success rates by 8.86 and 5.50 percentage points over no experience. Compared with raw interaction history, Skills and Lessons achieve comparable task performance at 53.0\% lower execution cost.

title: What Makes a Good Visual Representation for Spatial Understanding in MLLMs?
abstract: Spatial understanding is a necessary step in moving multimodal large language models (MLLMs) toward reasoning about the 3D physical world. Their visual pretraining data, however, is almost entirely 2D, so the visual tokens processed by MLLMs often lack inherent 3D structural information. A growing number of methods inject such structure by transferring representations from external vision or geometry models, and collectively establish that such transfer helps. Behind these methods lies a largely underexplored question: what makes a visual representation good for spatial understanding? To answer it, we first separate what is transferred from how it is transferred, and then trace the resulting differences back to properties of the representations themselves. What we transfer comes from 3D geometry models, self-supervised image and video models, vision-language models, and generative models, in the form of latent features or explicit depth and point maps. We transfer it either by distillation, using it as a supervision target, or by fusion, feeding it as an additional input. We find that a representation's 3D structure correlates strongly with how much it helps, measured by cross-view consistency for latent features and by depth and reconstruction accuracy for explicit geometry. We further show that the form of a representation dictates the mechanism it needs. Latent features gain as much from fusion as from distillation; explicit geometry gains little from fusion, and most of its distillation gain depends on a geometry decoding head. Guided by these findings, we distill both latent features and explicit geometry into a single MLLM. Taking only RGB video as input, it consistently improves over its base model on both static 3D and dynamic 4D spatial reasoning benchmarks.

title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.

title: Tiny Recursive Message Passing
abstract: Message passing neural networks have shown remarkable performance in algorithmic and constraint reasoning, due to their ability to encode the structure of the task directly in the architecture. Recent work has shown that better results can be achieved using recursive transformers trained with deep supervision and truncated recursions, which make extremely deep loops stable to train, and equipped with test-time procedures such as discrete deduction lattices. In this work, we apply the same procedures to message passing networks, and show that the two ingredients are complementary, and lead to parameter efficient models: we obtain about $99\%$ test accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme with a model of $16$k parameters that trains in about $10$ minutes on an H100, or in $9$ hours on a CPU. We further show that the cost of truncating gradients grows with the number of rounds information needs to cross the graph, making the choice of wiring a trade-off between robustness to truncation and transfer across problem sizes. We conclude by showing that our models transfer zero-shot to larger instances than those seen during training, outperforming popular neural baselines on N-queens and Boolean satisfiability with a fraction of their parameters.

title: Dynamic safety filters in reinforcement learning for robotic systems
abstract: Pri spodbujevalnem učenju se agent uči iz lastnih poskusov in postopno izboljšuje svojo strategijo, torej pravilo, ki vsakemu stanju priredi dejanje. V robotiki je tako učenje drago, saj napaka lahko pomeni poškodbo robota in tveganje za okolico. Nevarnost se običajno rešuje s statičnimi pravili, na primer s pragom na kotu, ta pa ne upoštevajo dinamike fizičnih sistemov: isti kot je lahko povsem varen ali že nepopravljivo izgubljen, odvisno od smeri gibanja in preostalega nadzora. V delu preizkušamo dinamično alternativo, pri kateri agent nevarnost oceni sam, brez zunanje opredelitve prepovedanih stanj. Osrednja mera je opolnomočenost: koliko različnih prihodnjih izidov lahko agent s svojimi dejanji še doseže, zato upade, ko agent izgublja nadzor. Oceno z utežjo prištejemo k nagradi za nalogo kot pomožno nagrado, tako da se agent uči tudi ohranjati nadzor. Za primerjavo vključimo še prediktivno informacijo, ki meri, koliko prihodnosti je mogoče razbrati iz preteklosti. Mehanizem preverjamo na determinističnem obrnjenem nihalu, ki ga mora agent z omejenim navorom pripeljati v ukazano lego in jo zadržati. Z vzvratno dosegljivostjo je mogoče za vsako stanje natančno izračunati, ali je padec, torej prekoračitev mejnega kota, ki konča epizodo, še mogoče preprečiti. To služi kot referenčna resnica o tveganju, delež učnih epizod s padcem pa kot merilo varnosti učenja. Učimo tako strategije za posamezen cilj kot eno strategijo za vse cilje. Analiza približno 3.000 učnih tekov prinese tri ugotovitve. Prvič, opolnomočenost tveganje zares zaznava: stanja razvrsti po nevarnosti občutno bolje kot katerakoli od obeh spremenljivk, iz katerih je izračunana (rangovna korelacija z izračunano referenco 0,70 proti 0,33 za kotno hitrost in 0,00 za kot nihala), prediktivna informacija pa na istem preizkusu odpove. Drugič, vpliv uteži ni sorazmeren kompromis, temveč ima optimum: pri zmernih vrednostih se padci med učenjem občutno zmanjšajo ob komaj opaznem upadu uspešnosti naloge, pri pretiranih pa pomožna nagrada prevlada nad nalogo in agent cilj opusti. Tretjič, pri strategiji za posamezen cilj korist ne izvira iz vsebine signala, saj jo enako dobro dosežeta kontroli brez informacijske vsebine, konstantna in naključno premešana pomožna nagrada. Pri enotni strategiji za vse cilje pa opolnomočenost korist obdrži in padce med učenjem zniža s 43,8 na 27,7 %, obe kontroli pa sta slabši od izhodišča brez pomožne nagrade. Notranji varnostni signal je torej učinkovit le, kadar je porazdelitev obiskanih stanj dovolj široka, da signal preko nje ohrani dovoljšnjo variabilnost

title: Haxion - r home computer system
abstract: *Current Security Posture of Haxion + Glyphon* We have built a deliberately hostile environment for unauthorized control: - Custom language (Glyphon) with ritualized safety invocations - Mandatory authority levels and authentication (including backslang) - Cryptographic script signatures - Independent safety microcontroller that the main OS cannot override - One-way telemetry only - Built-in antiviral scanning + scrubber - Persistent locked configuration - Tamper-evident audit log - Dry-run / simulation mode under restricted authority - Sensor plausibility checks and graceful degradation This makes opportunistic and remote attacks extremely difficult. The system is intentionally alien to normal tooling and forces any attacker into expensive, targeted work. It is *highly secure by design* for its intended use. It is not magic and still requires good physical security and supply-chain discipline. --- What would you like to do next? 1. Formal threat model (what we defend against well vs residual risks) 2. Kernel-side implementation outline for the antiviral + scrubber 3. More Glyphon examples (emergency, degraded mode, multi-script) System Integration Summary: Drone & Video Uplink Addendum We have officially appended a high-bandwidth real-time data uplink and drone video ingest channel to the Mnemosyne Procurement Model. This integration specifically bridges the physical, safety-first computing layer of GlyphonOS with the primary Mnemosyne intelligence framework. rainos was taken so we are glyphon os

title: A TYPOLOGY-INFORMED METHODOLOGICAL MODEL FOR BUILDING AN UZBEK–CHINESE PARALLEL CORPUS
abstract: Uzbek and Mandarin Chinese lie at opposite ends of the morphological spectrum: Uzbek is an agglutinative Turkic language with SOV order and a rich case system, whereas Chinese is an isolating Sino-Tibetan language with SVO order, function words and numeral classifiers, written without word boundaries. Our search did not identify a systematic, openly available Uzbek–Chinese parallel corpus; the only directly relevant study found builds a filtered, partly LLM-generated pseudo-parallel dataset from news crawls. This paper proposes a typology-informed methodological model for building such a corpus. It has five components: (1) a layered design separating a human-verified gold core, an automatic extension and a labelled synthetic layer, with provenance metadata; (2) asymmetric linguistic processing linked through Universal Dependencies; (3) multi-level alignment down to the morpheme, with correspondence-type labels; (4) a "unit–set of equivalents" lexical database; and (5) retrieval-augmented integration with large language models. A correspondence table and two author-composed sentence pairs show that most grammatical correspondences are not one-to-one. An evaluation protocol is specified for future empirical work.

title: A Python Laboratory for Private Synthetic Data and Privacy Models
abstract: This program demonstrates DataSynthesizer's PrivBayes, SmartNoise Synth's MST and AIM, and OpenDP's central counting and local randomised-response mechanisms using a fictional health survey. It generates synthetic records, evaluates selected statistical relationships and subgroup errors, and illustrates how trust assumptions differ between central, local and shuffle models. Public categorical domains control preprocessing, while meaningful checks verify output validity, encoding consistency and estimator behaviour. The shuffle demonstration permutes existing randomised reports without claiming an amplified privacy guarantee. The laboratory includes version reporting and example outputs; its exact diagnostic comparisons are intended for fictional data and are not automatically safe to release for confidential datasets.

title: An Investment Analysis Research Enhanced Enterprise Development Algorithm for Bankruptcy Prediction
abstract: Corporate bankruptcy prediction requires reliable optimization methods capable of identifying effective machine-learning configurations while maintaining robust global search performance. This study proposes an investment-analysis-inspired Enhanced Enterprise Development Optimizer (EED) for global optimization and KNN-based bankruptcy prediction. Rather than introducing additional generic perturbation operators, EED incorporates historical performance appraisal, covariance- and correlation-based search allocation, and drawdown-aware adaptive recovery into the original Enterprise Development Optimizer. The optimization performance of EED is evaluated on the CEC2017 and CEC2022 benchmark suites under five dimensional settings and compared with eleven competing algorithms. For CEC2017, F2 is excluded because of documented implementation inconsistencies and unstable numerical behavior, and the remaining 29 functions, namely F1 and F3–F30, are used in the evaluation. Each algorithm is independently executed 30 times, and the results are assessed using the mean and standard deviation, convergence and distribution analyses, the Friedman rank test, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. EED achieves the best or tied-best mean performance on 28, 27, and 23 of the 29 retained CEC2017 functions at 30, 50, and 100 dimensions, respectively, and on 9 and 8 of the 12 CEC2022 functions at 10 and 20 dimensions. Its overall Friedman mean rank is approximately 1.41, while the Wilcoxon comparison with the original ED yields 107 wins, 3 ties, and 1 loss, indicating that the proposed mechanisms provide consistent improvements across different benchmark landscapes rather than gains on only a small number of functions. To examine practical applicability, EED is further used to optimize the neighborhood size and distance measure of KNN on the Wieslaw and JPNBDS bankruptcy datasets. The resulting EED-KNN models show competitive and relatively stable performance in ACC, MCC, F1-score, and precision. The benchmark experiments therefore establish the general search capability and robustness of EED, while the bankruptcy-prediction application demonstrates that these optimization advantages can be transferred to a discrete machine-learning parameter-selection task.

title: Why Static Skill Inconsistencies Do Not Equate to Runtime Risks: A Behavioral Analysis of LLM Agent Execution
abstract: LLM agent frameworks heavily rely on external skill assets to standardize tool usage, encode operational workflows, and supply executable runtime resources. Despite their widespread adoption, multi-component skill packages frequently suffer from cross-artifact inconsistencies, where documentation, scripts, and configuration files specify conflicting behavioral constraints. Although static auditing techniques can uncover such contractual discrepancies, static defect volume cannot reliably reflect real-world agent performance degradation. This gap leaves practitioners without rigorous evidence to assess the practical risk of flawed agent skills. This paper presents a systematic empirical study to demystify the runtime implications of skill inconsistencies. We conduct large-scale auditing over 575 community and benchmark skills, yielding 1,182 manually validated contract inconsistencies. We further build a controlled evaluation pipeline with 49 executable agent tasks and three representative LLMs across NoSkill, OriginalSkill, and FixedSkill experimental settings. Through fine-grained behavioral analysis of 441 paired execution trajectories, we quantify the actual performance impacts of resolved defects.

title: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
abstract: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.

While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.

title: Multimodal Contrastive Representation Learning Based Voice Conversion for Electrolaryngeal Speech Enhancement
abstract: Electrolaryngeal (EL) speech suffers from severe acoustic mismatches with normal speech, resulting in degraded naturalness and intelligibility. These mismatches also make sequence-to-sequence voice conversion struggle to learn robust intermediate representations, hindering EL-speech-to-normal-speech conversion (EL2SP) performance. To address this, we propose a novel multimodal contrastive representation learning framework to 1) achieve richer multimodal-representation learning, and 2) facilitate the transferability of multimodal representations to speech-only EL2SP. First, EL speech and text representations are fused to learn multimodal representations for target speech generation, during which cross-modal contrastive learning is employed to encourage a semantically consistent speech--text representation space. Next, the fused representations are treated as a fixed target to guide speech-only representation learning through cross-stage contrastive learning, enabling multimodal knowledge to be transferred to the EL2SP task while preserving architectural and inference simplicity. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms both the speech-only and multimodal-based baselines.
